## Overview and reproducibility

This document compiles methodological details, supplementary analyses, and reproducibility outputs supporting the main manuscript.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}

It tests three preregistered hypotheses about the fungal community of willow ptarmigan dung across a seasonal contrast (winter, March vs. summer, June) replicated over three years (2022–2024):

-   **H1** — The dung fungal community differs in composition between the winter and summer timeblocks, and the magnitude of this seasonal shift is consistent across the three sampling years (2022–2024).
-   **H2** — Fungal alpha diversity is higher in summer than winter. On the diet-matched subset, per-sample fungal alpha diversity increases with per-sample dietary plant richness, consistent with diet acting as the dominant propagule source for the dung fungal community.
-   **H3** — On the diet-matched subset, individual fungal OTUs differ in *how specifically* they covary with the diet-plant community. Fungi tightly covarying with particular plant taxa are interpreted as likely ingested dietary passengers; taxonomically recognised coprophilous taxa (e.g. Sordariales) are expected to show diffuse, non-specific associations, consistent with their non-host-specific spore dispersal. Tight single-plant covariation is treated as the strong, interpretable signal.

Two exploratory aims accompany the preregistered hypotheses and are kept conceptually distinct from them:

-   **E1** — Identify fungal OTUs lacking a confident UNITE assignment that occur at non-trivial abundance ("dark taxa"); see Section 3.4.
-   **E2** — Document the occurrence and relative abundance of *Sporormiella*-type and other Sordariales taxa used in palynological reconstructions, to provide a modern avian reference point for a herbivore-presence proxy currently calibrated almost entirely on mammals; see Section 3.2. Note that E2 (a herbivore-presence proxy) is distinct from H3 (plant–fungus covariation) and from E1 (dark taxa).
:::

Computationally intensive steps (DADA2 denoising, LULU curation, iNEXT3D diversity estimation, GLLVM and Bayesian model fitting, phylogenetic community-structure null models) were executed on a remote Ubuntu-based computing environment. Their outputs (figures, tables, and selected model objects) are integrated here as static results, with the generating code shown in collapsible drop-downs in the HTML version.

All figures (PNG) and result tables (CSV) are stored within the project repository under `Supplementary/figures/` and `Supplementary/tables/` using relative paths. Rendering this document therefore requires cloning the repository and opening the `.qmd` file from the `Supplementary/` directory.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- project status; not part of the submitted appendix -->

## Status of this appendix

The analyses in **Sections 2–5** are finalized: they were regenerated end-to-end from the corrected canonical dataset and independently checked. **Section 6** (GLLVM, OTU-resolved H1) is integrated, with one flagged caveat — its fitted models predate the depth-filter correction (see the callout there). **Sections 7.1** (the Bayesian diet-richness mechanism for H2) and **7.2** (H3 OTU–plant covariation) are integrated. **Section 8** (functional guilds) is integrated and was regenerated from the corrected canonical dataset. **Section 9** (HMSC joint species distribution model) is integrated. **Section 10** collects the main-text figures and holds the authoritative build code for each; it is being populated as the main text is written.

**Correction of 2026-08-05 (affects a headline result).** The Section 4.2 PERMANOVA previously fitted `Year` as a numeric covariate rather than a factor, which tested only a linear trend across 2022–2024 and reported *no* Season × Year interaction. With `Year` correctly fitted as a factor the interaction is **significant** (R² = 0.10, p = 0.011): seasonal turnover is real and directionally consistent, but its magnitude differs among years. The Season main effect is unchanged. See the "Supersedes" note in Section 4.2, the new Table S5b, and Figure 2.
:::

## Section 1: Data and analysis objects {.unnumbered}

All downstream analyses draw on a small set of canonical phyloseq objects produced by `4_data_prep.R` and saved in `eco_analysis.RData` on the analysis server. Computationally intensive analyses were executed remotely; their outputs are stored under `tables/` and `figures/` and loaded/embedded as needed.

```{r load-objects}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true

load("eco_analysis.RData")  # produced by 4_data_prep.R

# alldat        : named list (nopool / pool / pspool). Primary analysis object.
#                 PCR replicates COLLAPSED by summing; non-fungal OTUs removed;
#                 taxonomy cleaned; depth filter >= 10,000 reads/sample.
#                 alldat$nopool = 52 samples (canonical object for PERMANOVA,
#                 iNEXT3D, dominance).
# alldat.rfy    : same as alldat but rarefied to the minimum depth (12,615 reads).
#                 Retained as a cross-check: per-sample Hill numbers are now
#                 size-standardised to that same depth analytically by iNEXT.3D
#                 from the raw counts, rather than read off one rarefaction draw.
# alldat_full   : one row per PCR replicate (never collapsed), pass-through depth
#                 threshold; for GLLVM / mixed-model work where PCR replicate is an
#                 explicit random effect (read-count offset, not rarefaction).
#
# The non-pooled (independent per-sample) DADA2 inference strategy ("nopool") is
# primary throughout, matching the numbered pipeline scripts.
```

## Section 2: Bioinformatics summary and study design

### 2.1 Study site and sampling design

Willow ptarmigan (*Lagopus lagopus*) faecal samples were collected at Lifjellet (Lierne municipality, Trøndelag, Norway) across a seasonal contrast: winter (March, snow-covered, browse-dominated diet) versus summer (June, green forage available) — replicated over three years (2022, 2023, 2024). The design is a Season × Year factorial, with repeated sampling of individually identifiable birds (microsatellite-confirmed where possible). Approximately 60 dung samples passed processing, of which \~31 have paired plant ITS2 diet data used for the H2 diet-richness mechanism (Section 7).

Each biological dung sample was amplified in two independent PCR replicates. DNA extraction, ITS2 amplification, demultiplexing (sabre), primer trimming (cutadapt), denoising (DADA2, non-pooled inference), and post-clustering curation (LULU) followed the workflow in `Scripts/1_demultiplexing.R`–`Scripts/3_taxonomic_assignment.R`; taxonomy was assigned against the UNITE reference (naïve Bayes, `minBoot = 80`). Negative, no-template, and extraction-blank controls were sequenced alongside samples and used for contaminant removal in `Scripts/4_data_prep.R`.

```{r tab-design}
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the Season x Year design table"
library(knitr)
# Counted from the canonical per-sample table so the design cannot drift from the
# object every downstream analysis uses (52 samples, PCR replicates summed).
des <- read.csv("tables/guild_composition_per_sample.csv", check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(des) == 52, !anyNA(des$Season), !anyNA(des$Year))

tab <- table(factor(des$Season, levels = c("Winter", "Summer")), des$Year)
out <- cbind(as.data.frame.matrix(addmargins(tab, 2)))
names(out)[ncol(out)] <- "Total"
out <- cbind(Season = c("Winter (March)", "Summer (June)"), out)
out <- rbind(out, c("Total", colSums(out[, -1, drop = FALSE])))

kable(out, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(out) - 1)),
      caption = "Table S1. Season x Year sampling design of the final analysis set: biological dung samples retained after PCR-replicate collapsing, decontamination, non-fungal OTU removal and the 10,000-read depth filter. Each sample was amplified in two independent PCR replicates. Five of the 57 samples entering the depth filter were dropped by it (Figure S1, Table S2).")
```

### 2.2 Read and OTU tracking through the pipeline

This section reports read and OTU retention through each processing step for the primary `nopool` strategy.

```{r tab-tracking}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

trk <- read.csv("tables/report_read_otu_tracking.csv", check.names = FALSE)
trk <- trk[trk$strategy == "nopool", ]

step_labels <- c(
  "post_cutadapt_input_to_filter"            = "Post-cutadapt (input to DADA2 quality filter)",
  "post_quality_filter"                       = "Post quality filter (filterAndTrim)",
  "post_merge_denoise"                        = "Post denoise + merge pairs (pre-chimera ASVs)",
  "post_chimera_removal"                      = "Post chimera removal (ASVs)",
  "post_LULU_curation"                        = "Post LULU curation (OTUs)",
  "pcr_collapsed_decontaminated_taxassigned"  = "PCR replicates collapsed, decontaminated, taxonomy assigned",
  "non_fungal_OTU_removal"                    = "Post non-fungal OTU removal (PlutoF)",
  "depth_filter_final (>=10,000 reads)"       = "Final analysis set (depth filter >= 10,000 reads/sample)"
)

first_reads <- trk$total_reads[1]
trk_out <- data.frame(
  `Pipeline step`        = step_labels[as.character(trk$step)],
  `Samples / wells`      = trk$n_samples,
  `OTUs (ASVs)`          = ifelse(is.na(trk$n_taxa), "—", format(trk$n_taxa, big.mark = ",")),
  `Total reads`          = format(round(trk$total_reads), big.mark = ","),
  `% of starting reads`  = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * trk$total_reads / first_reads),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)

kable(trk_out,
      caption = "Table S2. Reads and OTUs retained at each processing step (nopool strategy).")
```

**Figure S1**: Per-sample sequencing depth after non-fungal OTU removal, before the depth filter (57 samples). Five samples (four winter, one summer) fall below the 10,000-read cutoff and are excluded from the analysis-ready dataset (52 samples).

![](figures/report_library_depth.png)

```{r sec2-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full code for Table S2 and Figure S1 — the source of truth for the read/OTU tracking table and library-depth figure"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Table S2 (read/OTU tracking) and Figure S1 (library depth).
#
# This chunk is the source of truth for both: there is no parallel script.
# Nothing is re-run here -- every count is read from workspaces the pipeline
# already wrote. Raw-fastq and post-demultiplexing counts (script 1) are out of
# scope: no counts were logged for that step and recovering them means
# rescanning ~39 GB of FASTQ. The earliest quantified checkpoint is therefore
# "post-cutadapt reads entering DADA2 quality filtering".
#
# Sources (all read-only):
#   merged_ITS.RData                 2_DADA2_lulu.R, saved after LULU curation
#   phyloseq_comparison_summary.csv  4_data_prep.R Section 8
#   eco_analysis.RData               4_data_prep.R
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(phyloseq)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Data live outside the repo; set this to the directory holding the workspaces.
data_dir <- "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates"
tab_dir  <- "tables"; fig_dir <- "figures"   # relative to this .qmd

grDevices::pdf(NULL)                          # headless: no X11 fallback
save_png <- function(obj, filename, width, height, dpi = 800) {
  png(file.path(fig_dir, filename), width = width, height = height,
      units = "in", res = dpi)
  print(obj); dev.off()
}

# ---- Scripts 1-2: post-cutadapt / filter / merge / chimera / LULU ----------
e <- new.env(); load(file.path(data_dir, "merged_ITS.RData"), envir = e)
out_df <- e$out_df
reads_postcutadapt <- sum(out_df$reads.in)
reads_postfilter   <- sum(out_df$reads.out)

dims_of <- function(m) data.frame(n_samples = nrow(m), n_taxa = ncol(m),
                                  total_reads = sum(m))

step_merge <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(step = "post_merge_denoise", strategy = "nopool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtab)),
  data.frame(step = "post_merge_denoise", strategy = "pool",   dims_of(e$merged_seqtabPP)),
  data.frame(step = "post_merge_denoise", strategy = "pspool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtabpsPP)))
step_chimera <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(step = "post_chimera_removal", strategy = "nopool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtab.nochim)),
  data.frame(step = "post_chimera_removal", strategy = "pool",   dims_of(e$merged_seqtabPP.nochim)),
  data.frame(step = "post_chimera_removal", strategy = "pspool", dims_of(e$merged_seqtabpsPP.nochim)))
step_lulu <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(step = "post_LULU_curation", strategy = "nopool", dims_of(e$nopool.lulu)),
  data.frame(step = "post_LULU_curation", strategy = "pool",   dims_of(e$pool.lulu)),
  data.frame(step = "post_LULU_curation", strategy = "pspool", dims_of(e$pspool.lulu)))

# Sample count at the pre-DADA2 steps is the number of PCR wells: out_df rows
# are per read-direction (r1/r2), so strip that suffix before counting.
n_pcr_wells <- length(unique(sub("r[12]$", "", rownames(out_df))))
step_filter <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("nopool","pool","pspool"), function(s)
  data.frame(step = "post_cutadapt_input_to_filter", strategy = s,
             n_samples = n_pcr_wells, n_taxa = NA, total_reads = reads_postcutadapt)))
step_qfilter <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("nopool","pool","pspool"), function(s)
  data.frame(step = "post_quality_filter", strategy = s,
             n_samples = n_pcr_wells, n_taxa = NA, total_reads = reads_postfilter)))

rm(e); gc()

# ---- Scripts 3-4: PCR-collapsed/decontaminated -> non-fungal removal ->
#      depth filter, from 4_data_prep.R Section 8's comparison table ---------
cmp <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "phyloseq_comparison_summary.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cmp <- cmp[cmp$object %in% c("nopool","pool","pspool"), ]
relabel <- function(df, label)
  data.frame(step = label, strategy = df$object, n_samples = df$n_samples,
             n_taxa = df$n_taxa, total_reads = df$total_reads,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

tracking <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  step_filter, step_qfilter, step_merge, step_chimera, step_lulu,
  relabel(cmp[cmp$step == "initial", ],            "pcr_collapsed_decontaminated_taxassigned"),
  relabel(cmp[cmp$step == "post_PlutoF_filter", ], "non_fungal_OTU_removal"),
  relabel(cmp[cmp$step == "post_depth_filter", ],  "depth_filter_final (>=10,000 reads)")) %>%
  mutate(n_samples   = as.numeric(n_samples),
         n_taxa      = as.numeric(n_taxa),
         total_reads = as.numeric(total_reads)) %>%
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = c(
    "post_cutadapt_input_to_filter", "post_quality_filter", "post_merge_denoise",
    "post_chimera_removal", "post_LULU_curation",
    "pcr_collapsed_decontaminated_taxassigned", "non_fungal_OTU_removal",
    "depth_filter_final (>=10,000 reads)"))) %>%
  arrange(step, strategy)

write.csv(tracking, file.path(tab_dir, "report_read_otu_tracking.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Figure S1: per-sample depth at the post-non-fungal-removal checkpoint --
# That intermediate object is not saved in its own right, but is reconstructed
# exactly from two objects that are: the 57-sample pre-removal phyloseq and the
# already-computed non-fungal OTU id list.
load(file.path(data_dir, "eco_analysis.RData"))   # nopoolps.dada2, nonfungal_ids_by_strategy
ps_pp <- prune_taxa(setdiff(taxa_names(nopoolps.dada2),
                            nonfungal_ids_by_strategy$nopool), nopoolps.dada2)

depth_df <- data.frame(sample = sample_names(ps_pp), depth = sample_sums(ps_pp))
depth_df$Season <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps_pp))$Season
depth_df$status <- ifelse(depth_df$depth >= 10000,
                          "kept (>= 10,000 reads)", "dropped (< 10,000 reads)")

p_depth <- ggplot(depth_df, aes(reorder(sample, depth), depth, fill = status)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10000, linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("kept (>= 10,000 reads)"    = "#4C72B0",
                               "dropped (< 10,000 reads)"  = "#C44E52")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reads per sample (log scale)",
       title = "Library depth per sample (post non-fungal removal, pre depth filter, nopool)",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 6),
        legend.position = "top")

save_png(p_depth, "report_library_depth.png", width = 10, height = 5)

cat(sprintf("%d samples, %d dropped (<10,000 reads): %s\n",
            nrow(depth_df), sum(depth_df$status != "kept (>= 10,000 reads)"),
            paste(depth_df$sample[depth_df$status != "kept (>= 10,000 reads)"],
                  collapse = ", ")))
```

### 3.1 Community composition across ranks

Per-sample relative read abundance at four taxonomic ranks, with samples grouped and ordered by Season (and Year).

![](figures/phylum_barplot_ordered_season.png)

**Figure S2**: Phylum-level composition per sample, grouped by Season.

![](figures/class_barplot_ordered_season.png)

**Figure S3**: Class-level composition per sample, grouped by Season.

![](figures/Order_barplot_ordered_season.png)

**Figure S4**: Order-level composition per sample, grouped by Season.

![](figures/genus_barplot_ordered_season.png)

**Figure S5**: Genus-level composition per sample, grouped by Season. Many summer bars are dominated end-to-end by a single genus (*Thelebolus*, *Sporormiella*, or *Coniochaeta*), consistent with the dominance analysis in Section 5, whereas winter bars are more evenly patchworked across genera.

### 3.2 Coprophilous (dung-specialist) genera (E2)

This subsection addresses exploratory aim **E2**: documenting the occurrence and relative abundance of *Sporormiella*-type and other Sordariales taxa used in palynological herbivore-presence reconstructions, to provide a modern avian reference point for a proxy currently calibrated almost entirely on mammalian dung.

The canonical tax table was screened against a list of coprophilous genera comprising the standard palynological set — *Sordaria, Podospora, Cercophora, Chaetomium, Schizothecium, Preussia, Sporormiella, Delitschia, Pilobolus, Ascobolus, Coprinopsis, Saccobolus, Sporormia* — extended with four further dung-associated genera recovered here: *Thelebolus, Coniochaeta, Psathyrella* and *Stropharia*. This is the list used throughout this subsection, for both Table S3 and the read-share test below.

Six of the seventeen genera were detected, across 17 OTUs: ***Sporormiella*** (7 OTUs), ***Thelebolus*** (4), ***Psathyrella*** (2), ***Stropharia*** (2), and single OTUs of ***Coniochaeta*** and ***Coprinopsis***. The eleven remaining genera — including *Sordaria*, *Podospora* and *Cercophora*, the taxa most often counted in palynological work — do not appear in this dataset at all. Per-OTU winter/summer mean read shares and occurrences (number of samples per season, of 26 each) are shown below.

```{r tab-copro}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
copro <- read.csv("tables/report_coprophilous_by_season_v2.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(copro, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S3. Coprophilous-genus OTUs: mean read share (%) and occurrence per Season (canonical object, 52 samples; 26 winter / 26 summer).")
```

Total per-sample coprophilous read share is **markedly higher in summer** than winter — 45.7% versus 8.7% of reads on average (medians 47.5% and 0.02%; Wilcoxon rank-sum p = 0.0012). The contrast is carried by *Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta* and *Sporormiella*, the three summer-dominant OTUs of Section 5.4; *Psathyrella*, *Stropharia* and *Coprinopsis* occur only at trace level. Code for this table is shared with the dominance analysis and shown in Section 5.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}

### 3.4 Dark taxa and UNITE Species Hypothesis characterisation (E1)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- exploratory-status hedge -->

::: callout-warning
**Exploratory (E1); not yet definitive.** This subsection runs the authoritative UNITE `sh_matching` pipeline (v2.0.4, the service behind PlutoF) as a *complementary lens* on the taxonomically unresolved fraction of the community. It **does not modify the canonical taxonomy** used everywhere else in this appendix — Species Hypothesis (SH) matching and the DADA2/UNITE naïve-Bayes classifier answer different questions (which SH cluster and how novel, versus which confident Linnaean name) and are kept separate by design. Novelty calls and new-SH assignments here are preliminary and pending validation for the manuscript.
:::
:::

Nearly half of the retained fungal OTUs are **"dark taxa"**: 493 of 1129 (43.7%), accounting for 35.4% of reads that the naïve-Bayes classifier leaves without a confident genus. These are not spread evenly across the design: in the dominance analysis (Section 5.4), winter samples are markedly dark-taxa dominated, with dark taxa making up on average 51.3% of winter reads (a far smaller share in summer), and winter's single most persistent OTU (OTU1369) is itself a dark taxon. To make this unresolved winter community interpretable, every OTU's ITS2 sequence was matched against the UNITE SH reference set, which places each sequence into an existing species hypothesis or forms a new (candidate) one, independent of whether a Linnaean name is available.

```{r tab-e1-summary}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s <- read.csv("tables/E1_SH_assignment_summary.csv", check.names = FALSE)
e1_tab <- data.frame(
  Category = c("Dark OTUs (no confident genus)",
               " placeable to an existing named SH",
               " novel — forms a new species hypothesis",
               " no reference within 80% identity",
               " filtered before matching (QC)"),
  `Dark OTUs` = c(s$n_dark, s$placeable_existing_SH, s$novel_new_SH,
                  s$no_SH_match, s$excluded_nonITS),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(e1_tab,
      caption = sprintf("Table S-E1a. UNITE Species Hypothesis placement of the dark-taxa OTUs (no confident genus in the canonical taxonomy). Median best-hit similarity to UNITE = %.2f%%; %d dark OTUs gained a finer lineage (family or deeper) from the SH consensus. The last three rows are all non-placements: rows 3 and 4 differ only in whether a UNITE relative exists at 80%% identity, and row 5 covers sequences dropped by quality control before the matching step ran (see the caveats below for what that QC actually is). Main-text Fig. 5A merges rows 4 and 5.", s$median_similarity, s$gained_finer_lineage))
```

**Most dark taxa are close to known references, and a live-database cross-check further shrinks the genuinely-novel fraction.** Against the local reference, of the 493 dark OTUs 143 were placeable to an existing named UNITE SH, 247 formed new (candidate) species hypotheses, and 90 had no reference within 80% identity; 13 were dropped by quality control before matching. The novel and no-match sequences were then re-run through the PlutoF web service, whose reference database is larger and more current: this reclassified 79 formerly-novel OTUs across the community — 19 of them dark — as matches to existing named SHs (21 of the 79 resolving to species, and 11 of the 19 dark ones gaining a genus). Table S-E1a reflects this combined result: 162 placeable, 228 candidate-novel, 90 with no reference within 80%. It is worth being explicit that the last two are the same kind of outcome — neither sits inside an existing named SH — and that the 90 are the *most* divergent candidates rather than sequences that failed to analyse. The pipeline is designed to cluster them de novo into their own new Species Hypotheses, but in v2.0.4 the no-hits branch of `run_pipeline.sh` invokes the hits parsers (`parse_matches_sh.pl`) rather than `parse_matches_1.pl`, so the de-novo table (`matches_1_out_*.csv`) is never written and these OTUs reach `9_dark_taxa_SH_matching.R` as an absence rather than a status. Taken together, 331 of the 493 dark OTUs (67%) are candidate-novel in one form or the other. Each placeable OTU resolves to a stable SH page (`https://unite.ut.ee/sh/<code>`) carrying the taxon name and its DOI. The best-hit similarity distribution (Figure S-E1a) shows the dark fraction is bimodal — a spike near 100% (OTUs essentially identical to a reference but withheld a genus by the conservative `minBoot = 80` threshold) plus a real tail of divergent, candidate-novel lineages.

![](figures/E1_SH_similarity_hist.png)

**Figure S-E1a**: Best-hit similarity to the nearest UNITE Species Hypothesis, dark (no confident genus, red) versus named (grey) OTUs.

![](figures/E1_dark_taxa_novel_vs_placeable.png)

**Figure S-E1b**: Dark-taxa OTUs by SH placement category (placeable to an existing SH, novel/new SH, no reference within 80% identity, or filtered before matching). All four categories are kept separate here; main-text Fig. 5A merges the last two. Category names in the underlying `SH_class` column are unchanged (`no_SH_match`, `excluded_nonITS`).

SH matching directly addresses the "winter = dark taxa" caveat: 34.6% of the winter dark-read burden is placeable to an existing UNITE SH (mean of the per-sample ratio), while the remainder is candidate-novel. Expressed as shares of *all* winter reads rather than of the dark fraction — the form main-text Fig. 5B plots — the dark 51.3% divides into 15.8% placeable, 29.2% candidate-novel and 6.2% with no reference within 80% identity; the corresponding summer figures are 21.5%, 7.2% and 2.5% of a 31.2% dark fraction. Winter's dominant dark OTU, OTU1369, is genuinely novel: a candidate new SH only 85.4% similar to any reference, resolving no further than class Dothideomycetes.

**Toward permanent, citable identifiers.** Placeable taxa already carry citable UNITE SH identifiers (resolvable SH pages with DOIs). The candidate novel taxa are being registered: their representative ITS2 sequences are being deposited in a public archive (ENA) and imprinted as new SHs via PlutoF, which mints permanent DOIs — converting short-lived study detections into citable candidate species hypotheses (*registration in progress*; sequences in `models/E1_novel_taxa_for_plutof.fasta`).

```{r tab-e1-winter}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
w <- read.csv("tables/E1_winter_dominant_dark_taxa_SH.csv", check.names = FALSE)
w_disp <- w %>%
  transmute(
    OTU = OTU_ID,
    Class = sub("^c__", "", Class),
    `SH placement` = ifelse(!is.na(SH_URL), SH_code,
                     ifelse(SH_class == "novel_new_SH", "novel SH",
                     ifelse(SH_class == "no_SH_match", "no reference <80%", "filtered (QC)"))),
    `% id` = similarity_percentage,
    `Winter (n/26)` = paste0(winter_occ, "/", winter_n),
    `Winter %` = round(100 * winter_mean_share, 1),
    `Summer %` = round(100 * summer_mean_share, 1)) %>%
  head(12)
kable(w_disp, digits = 1,
      caption = "Table S-E1b. Top winter-abundant dark taxa and their UNITE SH placement. 'Winter %'/'Summer %' = mean per-sample read share within each season (26 samples each). Placeable SH codes resolve at https://unite.ut.ee/sh/<code>.")
```

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
#### Documentation notes — Section 3 {.unnumbered}

for section 3.1; Bars are seriated within each Season for readability. These panels use script 5's PCR-collapsed object (57 samples, no depth filter); the qualitative pattern is unaffected by the depth filter used elsewhere. These four panels are retained here in full because they are a different object and a different question from the main text: all four ranks, all 57 samples, no depth filter. The main-text genus panel (Fig. 1A, Section 10.1) shows the genus rank only, on the canonical depth-filtered 52-sample object, and on the same sample axis as the functional guilds.

section 3.4: Figure S-E1b is the same quantity as main-text **Fig. 5A** (Section 10.5), redrawn there with counts and percentages labelled — and, unlike here, with `no_SH_match` and the pre-matching exclusions merged into one "no reference within 80% id" bar. This section keeps all four categories; only the main figure bundles. Figure S-E1a (best-hit similarity, square-root axis normalised within each group so the divergent tail is legible beside the near-100% spike) was a main-text panel in an earlier version of Fig. 5 and is now supplementary only; Section 10.5 cites it for the bimodality claim. Main-text **Fig. 5C** plots Table S-E1b, which has no supplementary figure of its own, and **Fig. 5B** is the read-weighted seasonal view, built from `tables/E1_SH_readshare_by_sample.csv` (script 9 Section 4b) with no supplementary counterpart.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Caveats.** (i) "Excluded by ITSx" (`excluded_nonITS`, 21 OTUs across the dataset, 13 of them dark) is a misnomer inherited from the script's own comment. Reading `excluded_1.txt` by reason: **13 are vsearch coverage-chimera calls** (`CHIM`), 6 are ITSx chimeric/broken, 1 is under the 100 bp ITS2 length floor, and 1 is spurious. The 13 come from `exclude_chims.py`, whose rule is `perc_alignment_cov <= 85 AND perc_alignment_cov_target <= 85` — the *same* ≤85% coverage heuristic described in caveat (iii) below and treated there as unreliable, so it deserves the same scepticism here. **OTU320**, winter's third most abundant dark OTU, is one of these 13 — a `CHIM` call, not an ITSx one. (ii) The spurious exclusion is **OTU9**, which `matches_out_02.csv` places cleanly as `present_in SH0655188.10FU` (*Cladosporium herbarum*, with a resolvable SH page); it was flagged only by the "other eukaryotes" ITSx pass, which by construction finds no ITS in a fungal sequence. Because `excl_otus` is the first branch of the `case_when`, that flag wins. This is why the run log reports 554 `present_in` rows but 553 placeable OTUs. OTU9 is not a dark taxon, so no dark-taxa count and no panel of Fig. 5 is affected. (iii) On the PlutoF re-run, a reference-coverage heuristic flagged 248 of the resubmitted OTUs as putatively chimeric, but the *same* sequences passed cleanly in the local run and the flagged set is not the most-divergent one (median \~97% identity), so this flag is recorded (`plutof_chimera_flag`) but treated as unreliable and **not** used to exclude OTUs, pending scrutiny.
:::
:::

## Section 4: Community composition — H1 {.page-break-before}

H1 predicts seasonal compositional turnover of the dung mycobiome that is reproducible across years. Ordination and tests use **robust Aitchison distance** on the canonical depth-filtered object (`alldat$nopool`, 52 samples), as implemented in `vegan` 2.7.2, which completes the robust CLR matrix with a rank-3 OptSpace approximation before computing distances (Section 4.1); Table S7b repeats the tests on four full-rank distances. Four complementary analyses are reported: an unconstrained PCoA (visualization), a PERMANOVA with beta-dispersion check (Season × Year), a per-year breakdown of the seasonal contrast, and a distance-to-Season-centroid linear model (does within-season heterogeneity itself depend on year?).

### 4.1 Ordination

![](figures/PCoA_Aitchison_Season_canonical.png)

**Figure S6**: PCoA on robust Aitchison distances (unconstrained), canonical object, coloured by Season and shaped by Year. Crosses mark Season centroids; thin segments connect each sample to its Season centroid. The axis percentages are shares of the rank-3 reconstruction from which `vegan` computes this distance, not of the full community variation, which is why the axis titles name that denominator; under a full-rank Aitchison distance (CLR after a pseudocount) the same two axes take **13.7% and 9.5%** (23.2% together), and those are the closer approximation to the variance actually explained. See Section 4.1.

This is the same ordination as main-text **Fig. 2A** (Section 10.2).

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Reading the axis percentages.** The percentages on the PCoA axes are far larger than is usual for a microbiome ordination, and they must not be read as "the plot captures 89% of the community variation". They follow from how `vegan` constructs robust Aitchison distances. `decostand(x, "rclr")` treats zero counts as missing rather than as observed zeros and, whenever any are present — always true of an OTU table — completes the matrix with a **rank-3 OptSpace approximation** (`vegan:::.calc_rclr`, argument `ropt = 3`). The robust CLR matrix from which the distance is computed therefore has rank 3 *by construction*, and the resulting PCoA has exactly three non-zero eigenvalues rather than the 51 that 52 samples would otherwise allow. PCoA1 and PCoA2 take 58.0% and 31.3% of that three-dimensional reconstruction and PCoA3 the remaining 10.7%, so the two plotted axes cover most of a space that had already been truncated to three dimensions before the ordination began. The same table under a full-rank Aitchison distance (CLR after a pseudocount) gives the ordinary figures instead: 13.7% and 9.5%, or 23.2% for the two axes together. **The percentages describe the display, not an effect size.** Every inferential statement about H1 comes from the PERMANOVA of Section 4.2, and none of it depends on them.

**Why 58% on the first axis and 11% for Season are not in conflict.** The axis percentages and the PERMANOVA R² of Section 4.2 are computed from the same distance matrix and the same total inertia, but they answer different questions and are not comparable as effect sizes. A principal coordinate is *fitted* to absorb as much variance as possible along a single direction, with no reference to any grouping, and is therefore the largest share obtainable; Season is a fixed, externally specified two-group split, which has no reason to align with that direction. Decomposed axis by axis, Season accounts for 15.3% of the variance along PCoA1, 4.0% along PCoA2 and 10.3% along PCoA3 — that is 8.9%, 1.2% and 1.1% of the total, summing to the 11.2% that `adonis2()` reports for the Season term. A dominant first axis that is mostly *not* seasonal is the expected result rather than a contradiction: most of what separates these samples is something other than season.
:::

### 4.2 PERMANOVA and beta-dispersion

```{r tab-permanova}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
perm <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova.csv", check.names = FALSE)
perm <- perm[, c("term", "Df", "SumOfSqs", "R2", "F", "Pr(>F)")]
names(perm) <- c("Term", "Df", "SumOfSqs", "R2", "F", "Pr(>F)")
kable(perm, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S5. PERMANOVA (adonis2) on robust Aitchison distances, Season x Year, by terms. Year is fitted as a FACTOR (2 df), so the interaction tests genuine year-to-year differences in the seasonal contrast rather than a linear trend across the three years.")
```

Because the Season × Year term is significant, the seasonal contrast is also tested separately within each year:

```{r tab-permanova-by-year}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
py <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova_by_year.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Year               = py$Year,
  `n (W/S)`          = paste0(py$n_winter, "/", py$n_summer),
  `R²`               = round(py$R2, 3),
  F                  = round(py$F, 2),
  `p`                = py$p_value,
  `Centroid distance`= round(py$centroid_distance, 1),
  `Spread W`         = round(py$dispersion_winter, 1),
  `Spread S`         = round(py$dispersion_summer, 1),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S5b. Season effect tested within each year separately (PERMANOVA on robust Aitchison distances). 'Centroid distance' is the Euclidean distance between the winter and summer centroids in robust-CLR space that year — the magnitude of the seasonal shift. 'Spread' is the mean distance to the cell's own centroid.")
```

```{r tab-betadisper}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
bd <- read.csv("tables/report_betadisper.csv", check.names = FALSE)
bd <- bd[bd$term == "Groups", c("grouping", "Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq", "F", "Pr(>F)")]
names(bd) <- c("Grouping", "Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq", "F", "Pr(>F)")
kable(bd, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S6. Beta-dispersion (permutest of distance-to-centroid homogeneity) for Season and Year.")
```

### 4.3 Distance-to-Season-centroid (consistency across years)

```{r tab-centroid}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cen <- read.csv("tables/report_centroid_lm.csv", check.names = FALSE)
cen <- cen[cen$term != "Residuals", ]
names(cen) <- c("Term", "Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq", "F value", "Pr(>F)")
kable(cen, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S7. Linear model of each sample's distance to its Season centroid (robust CLR space) ~ Season * Year.")
```

Main-text **Fig. 2B** (Section 10.2) plots the distances behind this table, split by Season and Year; it reads its p-values from `tables/report_centroid_lm.csv`, so the figure and Table S7 are guaranteed to agree.

::: {.callout-note when-profile="docs" appearance="minimal"}
**H1 interpretation — the two clauses separate.** Season is a significant predictor of community composition (PERMANOVA R² = 0.11, F = 6.92, p = 0.002), so the **first clause of H1 (seasonal turnover exists) is supported**. The **second clause (magnitude consistent across years) is not**: the Season × Year interaction is significant and substantial (R² = 0.10, F = 3.20, p = 0.011), meaning the size of the seasonal contrast differs between years. That interaction is significant under four of the five distance measures of Table S7b but only marginal under the zeros-retained robust CLR (p = 0.061; caveat iii), so the safe reading is that constancy of magnitude is *not established*, rather than that year-to-year differences are proven.

Table S5b localises that interaction. The seasonal shift is strong in **2023** (R² = 0.24, p = 0.005; between-season centroid distance 35.7), much weaker in **2024** (R² = 0.14, p = 0.127; distance 10.3) and effectively absent in **2022** (R² = 0.02, p = 0.789; distance 6.9) — though this last figure is the one part of the breakdown that is sensitive to the distance measure, see caveat (iii) below. The *direction* of the shift is the same in all three years — it is the *magnitude* that varies, dominated by an unusually well-separated 2023. This is exactly the pattern the functional-guild analysis finds independently (Section 8.3: dung-saprotroph share summer versus winter is significant in 2023, marginal in 2024 and not significant in 2022).

The interaction is a difference in *location*, not merely in spread: the distance-to-Season-centroid model (Table S7) finds a strong Season effect on within-season spread (p \< 0.001) but **no** Season × Year interaction in that spread (p = 0.79). In other words, summer communities are consistently more heterogeneous than winter ones in every year, while how far apart the two seasons sit changes from year to year.

**Caveats.** (i) Beta-dispersion is significantly higher for summer than winter samples (F = 15.3, p = 0.002; Table S6), so part of the PERMANOVA R² reflects this difference in within-group spread rather than a pure centroid shift (Anderson 2001); this previews Section 5's finding that summer communities are individually more dominance-skewed. (ii) With three years and 15–19 samples per year, a single atypical year moves the interaction substantially; the per-year tests in Table S5b are correspondingly low-powered (no year has more than 10 samples per season). The safe reading is *"seasonal turnover is real and directionally consistent, but its magnitude is not established as constant across years"* rather than a positive claim about year-specific ecology.

(iii) The distance itself carries an assumption, and one specific claim above depends on it. As set out in Section 4.1, `vegan`'s robust Aitchison distance is computed from a rank-3 completion of the robust CLR matrix, so this PERMANOVA — like the ordination — is run on a three-dimensional reconstruction of the community rather than on its full dimensionality. Refitting the identical `Season * Year` model on full-rank distances gives the same qualitative verdict with smaller effect sizes:

```{r tab-permanova-sens}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sn <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova_sensitivity.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Distance            = sn$distance,
  Rank                = sn$rank,
  `Season R²`         = round(sn$season_R2, 3),
  `Season p`          = sn$season_p,
  `Year R²`           = round(sn$year_R2, 3),
  `Year p`            = sn$year_p,
  `Season × Year R²`  = round(sn$interaction_R2, 3),
  `Season × Year p`   = sn$interaction_p,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S7b. Sensitivity of the H1 PERMANOVA to the distance measure. All five rows are adonis2(d ~ Season * Year, by = 'terms') on the same canonical 52-sample object, 999 permutations, seed 20260805. 'Rank' is the number of non-negligible positive eigenvalues the distance admits: robust Aitchison is capped at 3 by vegan's rclr completion, the others are full-rank. 'Robust CLR, zeros retained' is the same robust CLR without that completion (log of the non-zero counts centred on their own mean, zeros left as zeros, as vegan computed it before version 2.7-1). The first row is the one reported in Table S5.")
```

The per-year breakdown is exposed to the same choice, and more sharply:

```{r tab-permanova-sens-year}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
library(knitr); library(tidyr)
sy <- read.csv("tables/report_permanova_sensitivity_by_year.csv", check.names = FALSE)
sy$cell <- sprintf("%.3f (p = %.3f)", sy$R2, sy$p_value)
wide <- pivot_wider(sy[, c("distance", "Year", "cell")], names_from = Year, values_from = cell)
names(wide)[1] <- "Distance"
kable(wide, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S7c. Season effect within each year, under each distance measure (R² with permutation p). Same models as Table S5b, refitted on each distance. The robust-Aitchison row is the identical test to Table S5b; its p-values differ in the third decimal (0.775 / 0.009 / 0.116 here against 0.789 / 0.005 / 0.127 there) only because each cell here is seeded independently, so the two draw different permutation sets. R² values are exact and match.")
```

The seasonal effect is robust to the choice of distance — Season is significant at p ≤ 0.002 under all five measures — but its reported R² sits at the top of its range and is better read as 0.055–0.11 than as a precise variance share. The Season × Year interaction is less secure than Table S5 alone suggests: it is significant under four of the five distances (R² = 0.05–0.10, p = 0.002–0.011) but only marginal under the zeros-retained robust CLR (R² = 0.044, p = 0.061), the full-rank member of the same robust-CLR family as the primary distance. The Year main effect changes significance in the opposite direction (p = 0.309 under the rank-3 distance, p = 0.004–0.032 under the full-rank measures), which is a further reason not to lean on it.

**One statement in this section needs qualifying.** The per-year breakdown's finding that 2022 shows essentially no seasonal shift (R² = 0.02, p = 0.789) is an artefact of the rank-3 distance. Under the three conventional full-rank measures (CLR with a pseudocount, Bray–Curtis, Jaccard) the 2022 contrast is modest but present (R² = 0.09–0.10, p ≤ 0.010); under the zeros-retained robust CLR it is of similar size but not resolved (R² = 0.07, p = 0.10), and the same holds for 2024 (R² = 0.09, p = 0.10), leaving only 2023 significant (R² = 0.14, p = 0.001; Table S7c). What survives every distance is the *ordering* — 2023 strongest (R² = 0.14–0.24), then 2024, then 2022 — and it is the size of the gap, not the ordering, that the rank-3 distance exaggerates. The defensible reading is that the seasonal shift was **largest in 2023** and smaller in 2022 and 2024, where it is detected under most but not all distances: the data show neither that it was absent in 2022 nor that its magnitude was constant across years. Section 8.3's independent guild result should be read the same way: it shares this ranking, but its non-significant 2022 cell is a question of power, not of a missing effect.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- records a correction to an earlier draft -->

::: callout-important
**Supersedes.** Earlier versions of this section reported no Season × Year interaction (p ≈ 0.95). That came from an error in the Section 4 analysis code, where `Year` was passed to `adonis2()` straight from `sample_data()` and so entered the model as a **numeric covariate (1 df)**, testing only a linear trend across 2022–2024 rather than the factorial interaction. `Year` is now fitted as a factor (2 df), as it always was in the distance-to-centroid model of Section 4.3. The Season main effect is essentially unchanged (R² = 0.112 in both); only the Year and Season × Year terms are affected. Corrected 2026-08-05; the same fix was applied to `Scripts/5_community_composition.R`, whose PERMANOVA is print-only.
:::
:::
:::

### 4.4 Turnover is compositional, not a shift in dominance

The PERMANOVA of Section 4.2 establishes that the two seasons differ, but not *how*: the same set of taxa redistributed among themselves would produce a significant Season term just as a genuine replacement of membership would. Table S7d separates the two readings in raw detections rather than through a distance, by asking how often the OTUs that shift most between seasons are found in the other season at all.

```{r tab-occupancy}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
oc <- read.csv("tables/report_season_occupancy.csv", check.names = FALSE)
pct <- function(x) ifelse(x == 0, "0",
                   ifelse(100 * x < 0.01, "<0.01", sprintf("%.2f", 100 * x)))
kable(data.frame(
  `Enriched in`      = oc$direction,
  OTU                = oc$OTU_ID,
  Taxon              = oc$Taxon,
  `Winter detections`= paste0(oc$prev_winter, "/", oc$n_winter),
  `Summer detections`= paste0(oc$prev_summer, "/", oc$n_summer),
  `Winter reads (%)` = pct(oc$share_winter),
  `Summer reads (%)` = pct(oc$share_summer),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lllccrr",
  caption = "Table S7d. Season occupancy of the twenty most seasonally-shifted OTUs, canonical object (alldat$nopool, 26 winter / 26 summer samples). Ranked by the difference in mean within-season relative read share; an OTU must be detected in at least 5 of the 26 samples of the season it is enriched in, so no single-sample bloom can enter the table. 'Detections' is the number of samples in which the OTU has a non-zero count; 'reads' is its mean share of a sample's reads within that season. Taxonomy is the finest confident UNITE rank, with the parent rank given in brackets where no genus was assigned.")
```

The two blocks are close to mutually exclusive. The ten winter-enriched OTUs account for **40.6%** of the reads of an average winter sample but **3.1%** of an average summer one; the ten summer-enriched OTUs account for **54.7%** of summer but **6.1%** of winter. Their cross-season detections are correspondingly sparse — a median of 3.5 of 26 summer samples for the winter-enriched set, and 1 of 26 winter samples for the summer-enriched set — and six of the twenty are never recovered in the opposite season at all. Across the whole object the same pattern holds at the level of bare presence: of 1,129 OTUs, only **171 (15%)** are detected in both seasons, against 265 winter-only and 693 summer-only.

This is corroborated by the distance-based tests, which do not depend on the ranking above. Recomputing the identical `Season * Year` PERMANOVA on presence/absence alone — discarding every abundance — leaves the seasonal effect essentially intact (Jaccard R² = 0.074, p = 0.001; Sørensen R² = 0.113, p = 0.001) against R² = 0.086 for the full-rank abundance-based Aitchison distance. Season explains as much of *who is there* as of *how much of each there is*.

Two qualifications. The blocks are defined by relative read share, so a taxon that is genuinely present but rare in the other season can still appear here as near-absent; the claim these numbers support is that the **dominant membership** of the two seasons is largely disjoint, not that the seasons share no taxa. And the winter-only/summer-only counts above are inflated by rare OTUs seen in a single sample: restricting to OTUs detected in at least five samples of a season leaves 9 winter-only, 51 summer-only and 11 shared, which preserves the asymmetry but on much smaller numbers.


```{r sec4-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full code for Section 4 — the source of truth for Figure S6 and Tables S5, S5b, S6, S7, S7b, S7c and S7d"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 4 (H1): PCoA, PERMANOVA, beta-dispersion, per-year breakdown,
# distance-to-centroid model, and the distance-measure sensitivity check.
#
# This chunk is the source of truth for every figure and table in Section 4;
# there is no parallel script. It reruns the Section 3-6 logic of
# 5_community_composition.R against the CANONICAL depth-filtered object
# (alldat$nopool, 52 samples) rather than that script's own unfiltered
# 57-sample object, and captures to CSV the statistics script 5 only prints.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(phyloseq); library(vegan); library(ggplot2); library(dplyr)

data_dir <- "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates"   # data live outside the repo
tab_dir  <- "tables"; fig_dir <- "figures"                  # relative to this .qmd
load(file.path(data_dir, "eco_analysis.RData"))

grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                        # headless: no X11 fallback
save_png <- function(obj, filename, width, height, dpi = 800) {
  png(file.path(fig_dir, filename), width = width, height = height,
      units = "in", res = dpi)
  print(obj); dev.off()
}

ps <- alldat$nopool    # canonical: 52 samples, >= 10,000 reads
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)

# ---- Figure S6: unconstrained PCoA on robust Aitchison distances -----------
d_ait <- vegdist(otu_mat, binary = FALSE, method = "robust.aitchison")
attr(d_ait, "Labels") <- rownames(otu_mat)   # vegdist drops Labels for robust.aitchison
ord   <- capscale(d_ait ~ 1)

# NB: rank 3, not 51. vegan's decostand(x, "rclr") treats zeros as missing and
# completes the matrix with a rank-3 OptSpace approximation (vegan:::.calc_rclr,
# ropt = 3), so this distance is Euclidean distance in a 3-D reconstruction and
# the PCoA has exactly three non-zero eigenvalues. There are NO negative
# eigenvalues -- the pmax() is a defensive no-op -- and the axis percentages are
# shares of that reconstruction, not of the full data. See Section 4.1.
eig  <- pmax(ord$CA$eig, 0)
ax1p <- round(100 * eig[1] / sum(eig), 1); ax2p <- round(100 * eig[2] / sum(eig), 1)

sc <- as.data.frame(scores(ord, display = "sites", choices = 1:2, scaling = 1))
colnames(sc)[1:2] <- c("Axis1", "Axis2"); sc$sample <- rownames(sc)
meta_p <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps)); meta_p$sample <- rownames(meta_p)
sc$Season <- droplevels(factor(meta_p$Season[match(sc$sample, meta_p$sample)]))
sc$Year   <- droplevels(factor(meta_p$Year[match(sc$sample, meta_p$sample)]))
cent <- aggregate(cbind(Axis1, Axis2) ~ Season, data = sc, FUN = mean)
names(cent) <- c("Season", "cX", "cY")
sc <- merge(sc, cent, by = "Season", all.x = TRUE)

gp_ait <- ggplot(sc, aes(Axis1, Axis2, colour = Season, shape = Year)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = cX, yend = cY, group = interaction(Season, sample)),
               alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = cent, aes(x = cX, y = cY, colour = Season), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 3, shape = 4, stroke = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  # Axis titles name the denominator on purpose: these percentages are shares of
  # the rank-3 rCLR reconstruction, not of the full community variation. Bare
  # "58.0%" reads as an effect size and invites comparison with the 11% Season R2.
  xlab(sprintf("PCoA1 (%.1f%% of rank-3 rCLR space)", ax1p)) +
  ylab(sprintf("PCoA2 (%.1f%% of rank-3 rCLR space)", ax2p)) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Robust Aitchison PCoA (canonical, depth-filtered, n=%d)",
                       nsamples(ps))) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Season", order = 1),
         shape  = guide_legend(title = "Year",   order = 2)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
save_png(gp_ait, "PCoA_Aitchison_Season_canonical.png", width = 12, height = 8)

# ---- Table S5: PERMANOVA (Season x Year) ----------------------------------
sampledf <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))
# Year is stored NUMERIC in sample_data. Left as-is it enters adonis2 as a
# continuous covariate (1 df), so `Season:Year` would test only a linear year
# trend rather than the factorial interaction H1 is about -- and it would
# disagree with the centroid model below, which factors Year. Factor both.
sampledf$Season <- factor(sampledf$Season)
sampledf$Year   <- factor(sampledf$Year)
dists <- vegdist(otu_mat, binary = FALSE, method = "robust.aitchison")

set.seed(20260805)   # permutation p-values -> reproducible committed CSV
perm <- adonis2(dists ~ Season * Year, by = "terms", data = sampledf)
perm_df <- as.data.frame(perm); perm_df$term <- rownames(perm_df)
write.csv(perm_df, file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Table S5b: the seasonal contrast within each year --------------------
# The Season x Year interaction is significant, so report WHERE the shift is
# strong. Also record the between-season centroid distance (the magnitude the
# interaction is about) and the per-cell mean distance to centroid.
rclr_py <- decostand(otu_mat, "rclr", MARGIN = 1)
dimnames(rclr_py) <- dimnames(otu_mat)   # vegan's rclr imputation drops dimnames
bd_cell <- betadisper(dists, interaction(sampledf$Season, sampledf$Year))
per_year <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(sampledf$Year), function(y) {
  i  <- sampledf$Year == y
  dy <- vegdist(otu_mat[i, , drop = FALSE], binary = FALSE, method = "robust.aitchison")
  a  <- adonis2(dy ~ Season, data = sampledf[i, , drop = FALSE])
  cw <- colMeans(rclr_py[i & sampledf$Season == "winter", , drop = FALSE])
  cs <- colMeans(rclr_py[i & sampledf$Season == "summer", , drop = FALSE])
  cell <- function(s) mean(bd_cell$distances[sampledf$Year == y & sampledf$Season == s])
  data.frame(Year = y,
             n_winter = sum(i & sampledf$Season == "winter"),
             n_summer = sum(i & sampledf$Season == "summer"),
             R2 = a$R2[1], F = a$F[1], p_value = a$`Pr(>F)`[1],
             centroid_distance = sqrt(sum((cw - cs)^2)),
             dispersion_winter = cell("winter"), dispersion_summer = cell("summer"),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
write.csv(per_year, file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova_by_year.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Table S6: beta-dispersion -------------------------------------------
beta  <- betadisper(dists, factor(sampledf$Season))
beta1 <- betadisper(dists, factor(sampledf$Year))
pt_season <- permutest(beta); pt_year <- permutest(beta1)
write.csv(dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(grouping = "Season", term = rownames(pt_season$tab), pt_season$tab,
             check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(grouping = "Year",   term = rownames(pt_year$tab),   pt_year$tab,
             check.names = FALSE)),
  file.path(tab_dir, "report_betadisper.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Table S7: distance to Season centroid (robust CLR space) ~ Season*Year -
rfyrg2 <- decostand(otu_mat, "rclr", MARGIN = 1)
dimnames(rfyrg2) <- dimnames(otu_mat)
meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(rfyrg2), rownames(meta)))

centroids <- rowsum(rfyrg2, group = meta$Season) / as.vector(table(meta$Season))
euclid <- function(x, y) sqrt(sum((x - y)^2))
meta$dist_centroid <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(rfyrg2)),
  function(k) euclid(rfyrg2[k, ], centroids[meta$Season[k], ]), numeric(1))
meta$Season <- factor(meta$Season); meta$Year <- factor(meta$Year)

mod <- lm(dist_centroid ~ Season * Year, data = meta)
centroid_anova <- anova(mod)
write.csv(data.frame(term = rownames(centroid_anova), centroid_anova, check.names = FALSE),
          file.path(tab_dir, "report_centroid_lm.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Tables S7b / S7c: sensitivity to the distance measure -----------------
# Robust Aitchison is computed from a rank-3 completion (see the ordination note
# above), which inflates both the axis percentages and the PERMANOVA R2. Refit
# the identical model on full-rank alternatives so Section 4.2 can state how
# much of the reported effect size depends on that choice.
#
# Placed at the END on purpose: the per-year adonis2 loop above does not reseed,
# so its permutation p-values depend on the RNG stream. Adding work before it
# would silently change already-committed outputs.
# Robust CLR WITHOUT matrix completion: log of the non-zero counts, centred on
# their own row mean, zeros left as zeros. This is what vegan < 2.7-1 computed for
# "rclr" / "robust.aitchison" and what most papers mean by robust Aitchison; from
# 2.7-1 vegan imputes the zeros by default (see Section 4.1). Written out
# explicitly so it does not depend on the installed vegan version.
rclr0 <- function(x) {
  l <- log(x); l[is.infinite(l)] <- NA
  r <- l - rowMeans(l, na.rm = TRUE); r[is.na(r)] <- 0; r
}

# The fifth entry is appended LAST on purpose: each entry reseeds, so adding it
# after the original four leaves their committed rows unchanged.
sens_dists <- list(
  "robust Aitchison (rank-3)"          = vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison"),
  "CLR + pseudocount (true Aitchison)" = dist(decostand(otu_mat + 1, "clr")),
  "Bray-Curtis"                        = vegdist(otu_mat, method = "bray"),
  "Jaccard (presence/absence)"         = vegdist(otu_mat, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
  "robust CLR, zeros retained"         = dist(rclr0(otu_mat)))

# Effective dimensionality: non-negligible positive eigenvalues of the classical
# MDS of each distance. Robust Aitchison returns 3 by construction.
dist_rank <- function(d) sum(cmdscale(d, k = nrow(otu_mat) - 1, eig = TRUE)$eig > 1e-8)

sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sens_dists), function(nm) {
  d <- sens_dists[[nm]]
  set.seed(20260805)
  a <- adonis2(d ~ Season * Year, by = "terms", data = sampledf)
  data.frame(distance = nm, rank = dist_rank(d),
             season_R2 = a$R2[1], season_F = a$F[1], season_p = a$`Pr(>F)`[1],
             year_R2 = a$R2[2], year_p = a$`Pr(>F)`[2],
             interaction_R2 = a$R2[3], interaction_p = a$`Pr(>F)`[3],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
write.csv(sens, file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova_sensitivity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Same check on the per-year breakdown: the claim that 2022 shows essentially no
# seasonal shift is the part most exposed to the rank-3 distance.
sens_year <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sens_dists), function(nm) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(sampledf$Year), function(y) {
    i <- sampledf$Year == y
    d <- switch(nm,
      "robust Aitchison (rank-3)"          = vegdist(otu_mat[i, , drop = FALSE], method = "robust.aitchison"),
      "CLR + pseudocount (true Aitchison)" = dist(decostand(otu_mat[i, , drop = FALSE] + 1, "clr")),
      "Bray-Curtis"                        = vegdist(otu_mat[i, , drop = FALSE], method = "bray"),
      "Jaccard (presence/absence)"         = vegdist(otu_mat[i, , drop = FALSE], method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
      "robust CLR, zeros retained"         = dist(rclr0(otu_mat[i, , drop = FALSE])))
    set.seed(20260805)
    a <- adonis2(d ~ Season, data = sampledf[i, , drop = FALSE])
    data.frame(distance = nm, Year = y, R2 = a$R2[1], F = a$F[1],
               p_value = a$`Pr(>F)`[1], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}))
write.csv(sens_year, file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova_sensitivity_by_year.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Table S7d: season occupancy of the most seasonally-shifted OTUs -------
# Section 4.2 establishes that the seasons differ; it does not distinguish a
# genuine replacement of membership from the same taxa redistributed among
# themselves. This table answers that in raw detections rather than through a
# distance. No RNG is involved, so it is safe at the end of the chunk.
#
# Ranked on the difference in mean within-season relative read share, with a
# floor of 5 detections in the enriched season so a single-sample bloom cannot
# enter the table.
is_w <- sampledf$Season == "winter"; is_s <- sampledf$Season == "summer"
rel  <- sweep(otu_mat, 1, rowSums(otu_mat), "/")

occ <- data.frame(
  OTU_ID       = colnames(otu_mat),
  share_winter = colMeans(rel[is_w, , drop = FALSE]),
  share_summer = colMeans(rel[is_s, , drop = FALSE]),
  prev_winter  = colSums(otu_mat[is_w, , drop = FALSE] > 0),
  prev_summer  = colSums(otu_mat[is_s, , drop = FALSE] > 0),
  n_winter     = sum(is_w), n_summer = sum(is_s),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
occ$share_diff <- occ$share_winter - occ$share_summer

# Finest confident rank. UNITE carries rank prefixes ("g__Thelebolus"); strip
# them or the lookup silently fails, and treat "unidentified" as missing.
tx <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tx[] <- lapply(tx, function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x))
tx[tx == "unidentified"] <- NA
k <- match(occ$OTU_ID, rownames(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix")))
occ$Taxon <- ifelse(!is.na(tx$Genus[k]), tx$Genus[k],
             ifelse(!is.na(tx$Order[k]), paste0("unassigned (", tx$Order[k], ")"),
             ifelse(!is.na(tx$Class[k]), paste0("unassigned (", tx$Class[k], ")"),
                    "unassigned")))
occ$Class <- tx$Class[k]

top_w <- occ[occ$prev_winter >= 5, ]; top_w <- head(top_w[order(-top_w$share_diff), ], 10)
top_s <- occ[occ$prev_summer >= 5, ]; top_s <- head(top_s[order( top_s$share_diff), ], 10)
write.csv(rbind(cbind(direction = "Winter-enriched", top_w),
                cbind(direction = "Summer-enriched", top_s)),
          file.path(tab_dir, "report_season_occupancy.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Community-wide occupancy counts quoted in the Section 4.4 text.
det_w <- colSums(otu_mat[is_w, , drop = FALSE] > 0)
det_s <- colSums(otu_mat[is_s, , drop = FALSE] > 0)
cat(sprintf("Detected both seasons: %d | winter only: %d | summer only: %d\n",
            sum(det_w > 0 & det_s > 0), sum(det_w > 0 & det_s == 0),
            sum(det_s > 0 & det_w == 0)))
cat(sprintf("At >= 5 detections in a season -- winter only %d, summer only %d, both %d\n",
            sum(det_w >= 5 & det_s == 0), sum(det_s >= 5 & det_w == 0),
            sum(det_w >= 5 & det_s >= 5)))

# The Sorensen figure quoted alongside Jaccard in Section 4.4. Same design,
# seed and permutation count as Tables S7b/S7c above.
set.seed(20260805)
a_sor <- adonis2(vegdist(otu_mat, method = "bray", binary = TRUE) ~ Season * Year,
                 by = "terms", data = sampledf)
cat(sprintf("Sorensen (presence/absence): Season R2 = %.3f, p = %.3f\n",
            a_sor$R2[1], a_sor$`Pr(>F)`[1]))
```
