## Section 5: Diversity — H2 {.page-break-before}

H2 predicts higher summer alpha diversity, tracking the richer summer diet. Two levels of analysis are presented together deliberately, because they appear to disagree in an informative way: the **pooled-season** estimate of 5.1 (which pools samples within a Season and asks about the Season's total species pool) versus the **per-sample** estimate of 5.2 (which asks about diversity within a single dropping and rewards evenness). Both are computed with iNEXT3D, so the disagreement cannot be an artefact of using two different estimators — 5.1 standardises by coverage across the two pooled incidence sets, 5.2 standardises by size across the 52 individual samples. The disagreement is resolved by the dominance analysis in 5.3.

Per-sample Hill numbers are size-standardised to a common depth of 12,615 reads — the minimum library size — using `iNEXT.3D::estimate3D(base = "size")` on the raw counts. This returns the analytic expectation of the Hill number at that depth, rather than the value observed in one random rarefaction draw, so the estimate is deterministic and uses the full read depth of every sample. Coverage-based standardisation is deliberately **not** used at the per-sample level: estimated sample coverage is ≥ 0.99999 in all 52 samples (exactly 1 in 46 of them, since 43 contain no singleton OTUs at all), which leaves coverage-based and asymptotic estimators either undefined or equal to the observed richness, and would reintroduce the dependence on sequencing depth that standardisation is there to remove.

### 5.1 iNEXT3D: coverage-based taxonomic diversity

Incidence (presence in a dropping) depends on read depth, and summer libraries are about 2.6 times deeper than winter ones (median 551,236 vs 209,602 reads). The pooled comparison is therefore made with depth held equal: every sample is rarefied to the canonical minimum of 12,615 reads before the incidence matrices are built, both Seasons are compared at one common sample coverage (0.65), and the whole procedure is repeated over 50 independent rarefaction draws. Table S8 reports the median over draws of each estimate and of its bootstrap 95% CI. Asymptotic (extrapolated) estimates are not used for inference, because with 26 droppings per Season they extrapolate to roughly twice the observed richness.

![](figures/H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season_rarefied.png)

**Figure S7**: iNEXT3D coverage-based rarefaction/extrapolation of taxonomic Hill numbers (q = 0, 1, 2), samples pooled within each Season (incidence data, nboot = 200), after rarefying every sample to 12,615 reads. The curves are drawn for the one rarefaction draw whose summer/winter ratio at q = 0 is closest to the median over 50 draws. Summer exceeds winter at every q.

```{r tab-inext}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s8 <- read.csv("tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_rarefied.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Season = s8$Season, q = s8$Order.q,
  `Estimate` = round(s8$qTD, 1),
  `95% CI` = sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", s8$qTD.LCL, s8$qTD.UCL),
  `Summer/winter` = ifelse(s8$Season == "Summer",
                           sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", s8$ratio_summer_winter_median,
                                   s8$ratio_draw_2.5, s8$ratio_draw_97.5), ""),
  `Draws with separated CIs` = ifelse(s8$Season == "Summer",
                                      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * s8$share_draws_CI_separated), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S8. Pooled-season taxonomic Hill diversity at equal sequencing depth and equal sample coverage (iNEXT3D, incidence data; every sample rarefied to 12,615 reads; coverage 0.65; 50 rarefaction draws, 100 bootstraps each). Estimate and CI are medians over draws. 'Summer/winter' is the median ratio of the two estimates with the 2.5–97.5% range across draws. The last column is the share of draws in which the two Seasons' 95% CIs do not overlap.")
```

The depth-controlled estimates in Table S8 are plotted as main-text **Fig. 4A** (Section 10.4). Summer is the richer pooled assemblage at every order, by a factor of 1.42 at q = 0, 1.57 at q = 1 and 1.78 at q = 2.

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Raw-count and asymptotic versions (superseded as the primary result).** Without rarefying first, the same coverage-standardised comparison gives summer/winter ratios of 1.73, 1.96 and 2.28 (`tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_standardised.csv`), i.e. about a fifth of the raw summer advantage is the depth difference. The asymptotic estimates below were the Table S8 of earlier drafts; they carry the same depth confound and extrapolate to about twice the observed richness (summer 1,708 vs 864 observed; winter 1,046 vs 436), which is the regime in which asymptotic richness is least reliable.

![](figures/H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season.png)

```{r tab-inext-asy}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
inx <- read.csv("tables/H2_iNEXT3D_TD_asymptotic.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(inx, digits = 2,
      caption = "Table S8b. iNEXT3D asymptotic taxonomic-diversity estimates by Season on raw (unrarefied) incidence (Hill q = 0, 1, 2; observed and asymptotic, with s.e. and 95% CI). Not used for inference.")
```
::::

### 5.2 Per-sample Hill diversity

![](figures/H2_hill_boxplot_Season.png)

**Figure S8**: Per-sample Hill numbers (PCR-collapsed object, size-standardised with iNEXT3D to the minimum sample depth of 12,615 reads). Winter exceeds summer at q1/q2 (Shannon/Simpson); summer has the higher mean at q0 (richness), but that difference is weak and depends on the model family (Tables S9, S9b).

This is the same quantity as main-text **Fig. 4B** (Section 10.4), which redraws it to the main-figure specification: annotated with the Table S9 contrasts below, and stacked beneath the pooled estimates of Fig. 4A on a shared set of facet columns. Figure S8 is retained here as the plain, unannotated view.

The Season effect is tested on the plotted values themselves: one size-standardised value per dung sample (n = 52), with a gamma GLM (log link) of `q ~ Season + Year`, so the Season coefficient is a summer/winter ratio adjusted for year. Year is a fixed effect (three levels are too few to estimate a variance), and individual bird is not modelled because only three birds were sampled more than once. The Season × Year interaction is tested by F-test and ΔAICc against the additive model.

```{r tab-lmm}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s9 <- read.csv("tables/H2_season_effect_per_sample.csv", check.names = FALSE)
pf <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
kable(data.frame(
  q = s9$metric, n = s9$n,
  `Mean winter` = round(s9$mean_winter, 1), `Mean summer` = round(s9$mean_summer, 1),
  `Summer/winter (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", s9$ratio_summer_winter,
                                     s9$ratio_lwr, s9$ratio_upr),
  `F (Season)` = round(s9$F_season, 2), `p (Season)` = pf(s9$p_season),
  `p (Year)` = pf(s9$p_year), `p (Season × Year)` = pf(s9$p_season_x_year),
  `ΔAICc (interaction)` = round(s9$dAICc_interaction, 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S9. Season effect on per-sample Hill diversity (gamma GLM, log link, q ~ Season + Year; n = 52 dung samples, size-standardised to 12,615 reads). The ratio is summer/winter adjusted for year, with a Wald 95% CI; p-values are F-tests. The Season × Year interaction is tested against the additive model; positive ΔAICc means the interaction is not supported.")
```

```{r tab-lmm-family}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
s9b <- read.csv("tables/H2_season_effect_family_sensitivity.csv", check.names = FALSE)
pf <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
kable(data.frame(
  q = s9b$metric,
  Gaussian = pf(s9b$p_gaussian), `Log-normal` = pf(s9b$p_lognormal),
  `Gamma (Table S9)` = pf(s9b$p_gamma), `Wilcoxon (unadjusted)` = pf(s9b$p_wilcoxon),
  `AIC Gaussian` = round(s9b$AIC_gaussian, 1), `AIC log-normal` = round(s9b$AIC_lognormal, 1),
  `AIC gamma` = round(s9b$AIC_gamma, 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S9b. Sensitivity of the Season test to the error family (Season p-value, same Season + Year model; Wilcoxon rank-sum without Year). AIC is on the response scale; the log-normal value includes the Jacobian term so it is comparable with the others.")
```

The two abundance-weighted orders are unambiguous: a winter dropping holds about 2.2 times (q = 1) and 2.5 times (q = 2) the effective number of OTUs of a summer one, under every family (p ≤ 0.005) and in every year (no Season × Year interaction). Richness (q = 0) is not: summer's mean is higher (48.3 vs 31.3 OTUs at equal depth), but the difference is significant only under the gamma model (p = 0.026, the AIC-preferred family for q = 0) and not under the Gaussian (p = 0.063), log-normal (p = 0.29) or rank-based (p = 0.11) tests. It is carried by a minority of very rich summer samples (summer median 35.6 vs winter 25.8).

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Replicate-level model (superseded as Table S9).** Earlier drafts tested Season with linear mixed models on PCR replicates (n = 98, each replicate size-standardised to 10,609 reads) with random intercepts for dung sample and, where estimable, Year and individual bird, dropping terms that went singular. That fitted a different unit and depth from the one plotted, and used a different random-effects structure at q = 0 (Year dropped after singular fits) than at q = 1–2. Retained for reference:

```{r tab-lmm-pcr}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
lmm <- read.csv("tables/H2_lmm_season_effect.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(lmm, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S9c. Replicate-level mixed-model Season effect (summer minus winter) on per-replicate Hill diversity, with 95% CI and p. Superseded by Table S9.")
```
::::

### 5.3 Why the two metrics disagree: dominance and evenness

The crossover is not an artifact, and it is not a difference of estimator — both levels are iNEXT3D. Pooling a Season's samples rewards the total species list (summer's samples collectively contain more species, so summer wins at every q). Per-sample q1/q2 instead downweight rare taxa and reward *within-sample evenness* — and individual summer samples are far more dominance-skewed than winter ones, so a single summer sample's effective diversity is lower even where its species list is longer.

```{r tab-dominance}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
dom <- read.csv("tables/report_dominance_summary.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(dom) <- c("Season", "n", "Mean richness (q0, 12,615 reads)", "Mean top-1 OTU share (%)",
                "Mean Pielou J", "Wilcoxon p (richness)",
                "Wilcoxon p (top-1 share)", "Wilcoxon p (evenness J)")
kable(dom, digits = 3,
      caption = "Table S10. Per-sample richness, top-1-OTU dominance, and Pielou evenness by Season, with Wilcoxon tests (canonical object, 52 samples). Richness is size-standardised to 12,615 reads (the q0 of Figure S8), because summer libraries are about 2.6 times deeper; top-1 share is a proportion and does not depend on depth, and Pielou J agrees with a size-standardised evenness, ln(q1)/ln(q0), at r = 0.995.")
```

Concretely: a summer sample's single most abundant OTU accounts for **56%** of its reads on average (vs **25%** in winter, p \< 0.001), and Pielou evenness is correspondingly much lower (J = 0.38 summer vs 0.72 winter, p \< 0.001). Summer's pooled species list is longer (the long tail iNEXT3D detects across droppings), while within a dropping one or two OTUs dominate the read count — evenness collapses, and q1/q2 track evenness more than richness.

### 5.4 Which OTUs dominate each Season?

```{r tab-top5}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
top5 <- read.csv("tables/report_top5_otu_by_season.csv", check.names = FALSE)
clean_tax <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v) | v == "", "—", sub("^[a-z]__", "", v))
top5$Season  <- tools::toTitleCase(top5$Season)
top5$Order   <- clean_tax(top5$Order)
top5$Genus   <- clean_tax(top5$Genus)
top5$Species <- clean_tax(top5$Species)
top5 <- top5[, c("Season", "OTU", "mean_pct_share", "Order", "Genus", "Species")]
names(top5) <- c("Season", "OTU", "Mean % share (within-season)", "Order", "Genus", "Species")
kable(top5, digits = 2,
      caption = "Table S11. Top-5 dominant OTUs per Season by mean within-season read share, with taxonomy.")
```

Summer's dominance is driven by three strongly season-skewed OTUs: **OTU1 (*Thelebolus*)** averages 24.9% of summer reads (15/26 summer samples vs 5/26 winter at 3.2%), **OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*)** is essentially summer-only (10.1% vs 0.2%), and **OTU636 (*Sporormiella* cf. *intermedia*)** is also summer-skewed (9.0% vs 2.5%). Winter's own top OTU, **OTU1369**, is a "dark taxon" (unclassified below Class, Dothideomycetes), present in 20/26 winter samples but only 3/26 summer, at 11.2% mean winter share.

```{r sec5-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full code for Section 5 — the source of truth for Figures S7 and S8, Tables S8–S11, and the coprophilous screen behind Table S3"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 5 (H2): coverage-based iNEXT3D diversity, per-sample and
# per-PCR-replicate Hill numbers, the frequentist mixed model, and the
# dominance / evenness / top-5 / coprophilous analyses.
#
# This chunk is the source of truth for every figure and table in Section 5,
# and for Table S3 in Section 3.2; there is no parallel script. Sections 1-2
# below reproduce 6_diversity_analyses.R Part A (Sections 1-2 plus the
# per-sample Hill block) run against the corrected canonical workspace,
# without the slow parts Section 5 does not need (the Bayesian diet-richness
# mechanism of Section 7.1, and Part B's phylogenetic null models).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(phyloseq); library(iNEXT.3D)
# Size-standardised Hill numbers: single source, shared with the fig4-build
# chunk and mirrored verbatim in Scripts/6_diversity_analyses.R.
source("hill_size_helper.R")
library(lme4); library(lmerTest); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)

data_dir <- "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates"   # data live outside the repo
tab_dir  <- "tables"; fig_dir <- "figures"                  # relative to this .qmd
load(file.path(data_dir, "eco_analysis.RData"))

grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                        # headless: no X11 fallback
save_png <- function(obj, filename, width, height, dpi = 800) {
  png(file.path(fig_dir, filename), width = width, height = height,
      units = "in", res = dpi)
  print(obj); dev.off()
}
otu_mat_of <- function(ps) {
  m <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) m <- t(m); m
}
# indivID is NA for samples without a confirmed microsatellite match; a unique
# placeholder makes each an unshared singleton random intercept instead of
# silently pooling unrelated unidentified individuals. Same convention as
# indivID_glm in 7_gllvm.R.
add_indivID_glm <- function(md) {
  md$indivID_glm <- droplevels(factor(ifelse(is.na(md$indivID) | md$indivID == "",
                                             paste0("unk_", md$sample), md$indivID)))
  md
}

# ===========================================================================
# Table S8b (secondary) / raw-count curves -- iNEXT3D coverage-based taxonomic Hill diversity
# ===========================================================================
ps  <- alldat$nopool
sd  <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps))
OTU <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) OTU <- t(OTU)

# Incidence matrices (species x sampling units), one per Season
inc_by_season_TD <- lapply(split(rownames(sd), sd$Season), function(samps) {
  M <- OTU[, colnames(OTU) %in% samps, drop = FALSE]
  M[M > 0] <- 1L; storage.mode(M) <- "numeric"; M
})

set.seed(1)
out_TD <- iNEXT3D(data = inc_by_season_TD, diversity = "TD", q = c(0, 1, 2),
                  datatype = "incidence_raw", nboot = 500)

labs_map <- c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer"); lvl_order <- c("Winter", "Summer")
.relabel <- function(df) {
  if (!("Assemblage" %in% names(df))) return(df)
  df$Assemblage <- factor(labs_map[df$Assemblage], levels = lvl_order); df
}
out_TD$TDInfo   <- .relabel(as.data.frame(out_TD$TDInfo))
out_TD$TDAsyEst <- .relabel(as.data.frame(out_TD$TDAsyEst))
if (!is.null(out_TD$TDiNextEst))
  out_TD$TDiNextEst <- lapply(out_TD$TDiNextEst, function(d) .relabel(as.data.frame(d)))

write.csv(as.data.frame(out_TD$TDAsyEst),
          file.path(tab_dir, "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_asymptotic.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

p_TD <- ggiNEXT3D(out_TD, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q") +
  labs(x = "Sampling units") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title = element_blank(), legend.title = element_blank())
save_png(p_TD, "H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season.png", width = 10, height = 6)

# Coverage-standardised comparison at the shared minimum coverage, so the two
# Seasons are compared at equal completeness rather than equal sample size.
Cmin <- min(as.data.frame(out_TD$TDInfo)[["SC(T)"]])
est_TD <- estimate3D(inc_by_season_TD, diversity = "TD", q = c(0, 1, 2),
                     datatype = "incidence_raw", base = "coverage",
                     level = Cmin, nboot = 500)
write.csv(est_TD, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_standardised.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Table S8 (primary) -- the same comparison with sequencing depth held equal
# The incidence matrices above record whether an OTU was DETECTED in a dropping,
# and detection rises with read depth. Summer libraries are ~2.6x deeper than
# winter ones (median 551k vs 210k reads), so on raw counts the pooled summer
# advantage is partly a depth effect. Here every sample is first rarefied to the
# canonical minimum depth (12,615 reads) and the coverage-standardised comparison
# is repeated over NDRAW independent draws, all at ONE common coverage level (the
# lowest sample coverage reached by either Season in any draw, rounded down), so
# the draws are comparable. Reported: the median over draws of the estimate and
# of its bootstrap 95% CI. Asymptotic estimates (above, now secondary) are not
# used for inference: they extrapolate to ~2x the observed richness.
# Placed AFTER the raw-count block so the seeded outputs above are unchanged;
# each draw has its own seed.
NDRAW <- 50
X_sxo <- t(OTU)                                     # samples x OTUs, raw counts
rar_depth_pool <- min(rowSums(X_sxo))
inc_of <- function(M) lapply(split(rownames(sd), sd$Season), function(samps) {
  I <- t((M[samps, , drop = FALSE] > 0) * 1)        # OTUs x sampling units
  storage.mode(I) <- "numeric"; I[rowSums(I) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
})
rar_draws <- lapply(seq_len(NDRAW), function(k) {
  set.seed(20260929 + k); inc_of(vegan::rrarefy(X_sxo, rar_depth_pool))
})
sc_draw  <- vapply(rar_draws, function(L)
  min(DataInfo3D(L, diversity = "TD", datatype = "incidence_raw")[["SC(T)"]]), numeric(1))
C_common <- floor(100 * min(sc_draw)) / 100
est_rar <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(NDRAW), function(k) {
  set.seed(20260929 + k)
  e <- estimate3D(rar_draws[[k]], diversity = "TD", q = c(0, 1, 2),
                  datatype = "incidence_raw", base = "coverage",
                  level = C_common, nboot = 100)
  e$draw <- k; e
}))
write.csv(est_rar, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_rarefied_draws.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
s8 <- aggregate(cbind(qTD, qTD.LCL, qTD.UCL) ~ Assemblage + Order.q, est_rar, median)
s8$SC <- C_common; s8$depth <- rar_depth_pool; s8$n_draws <- NDRAW
s8$Season <- factor(labs_map[s8$Assemblage], levels = lvl_order)
wide <- reshape(est_rar[, c("Assemblage", "Order.q", "qTD", "draw")],
                idvar = c("Order.q", "draw"), timevar = "Assemblage", direction = "wide")
rq <- tapply(wide$qTD.summer / wide$qTD.winter, wide$Order.q,
             quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
s8$ratio_summer_winter_median <- NA_real_
s8$ratio_draw_2.5 <- NA_real_; s8$ratio_draw_97.5 <- NA_real_
for (q in names(rq)) {
  i <- s8$Order.q == as.numeric(q)
  s8[i, c("ratio_draw_2.5", "ratio_summer_winter_median", "ratio_draw_97.5")] <-
    matrix(rq[[q]], nrow = sum(i), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
}
# Share of draws in which the two Seasons' 95% CIs are separated, per order q.
sep <- reshape(est_rar[, c("Assemblage", "Order.q", "qTD.LCL", "qTD.UCL", "draw")],
               idvar = c("Order.q", "draw"), timevar = "Assemblage", direction = "wide")
sep_share <- tapply(sep$qTD.LCL.summer > sep$qTD.UCL.winter, sep$Order.q, mean)
s8$share_draws_CI_separated <- as.numeric(sep_share[as.character(s8$Order.q)])
s8 <- s8[order(s8$Order.q, s8$Season), c("Season", "Order.q", "SC", "depth", "n_draws",
         "qTD", "qTD.LCL", "qTD.UCL", "ratio_summer_winter_median", "ratio_draw_2.5",
         "ratio_draw_97.5", "share_draws_CI_separated")]
write.csv(s8, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_iNEXT3D_TD_coverage_rarefied.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Figure S7 companion: rarefaction/extrapolation curves on the ONE draw whose q0
# summer/winter ratio sits closest to the median over draws, so the curves shown
# are representative of the depth-controlled estimates in Table S8.
r0 <- wide[wide$Order.q == 0, ]
k_rep <- r0$draw[which.min(abs(r0$qTD.summer / r0$qTD.winter - rq[["0"]][2]))]
set.seed(20260929 + k_rep)
out_rep <- iNEXT3D(data = rar_draws[[k_rep]], diversity = "TD", q = c(0, 1, 2),
                   datatype = "incidence_raw", nboot = 200)
if (!is.null(out_rep$TDiNextEst))
  out_rep$TDiNextEst <- lapply(out_rep$TDiNextEst, function(d) .relabel(as.data.frame(d)))
p_TD_rar <- ggiNEXT3D(out_rep, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q") +
  labs(x = "Sampling units (droppings)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title = element_blank(), legend.title = element_blank())
save_png(p_TD_rar, "H2_iNEXT_TD_by_Season_rarefied.png", width = 10, height = 6)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S9c (superseded) -- per-PCR-replicate Hill diversity + frequentist mixed model
# ===========================================================================
# alldat_full[[1]] is one row per PCR replicate and is deliberately NOT
# depth-filtered at the object level (4_data_prep.R uses a pass-through
# threshold, since it is built for read-count-offset models). Hill numbers need
# comparable effort across rows, so the canonical 10,000-read floor is applied
# here at the REPLICATE level, then everything is size-standardised (iNEXT.3D)
# to the minimum retained depth.
PCR_MIN_DEPTH <- 10000
ps_pcr <- prune_samples(sample_sums(alldat_full[[1]]) >= PCR_MIN_DEPTH, alldat_full[[1]])
ps_pcr <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps_pcr) > 0, ps_pcr)

rar_depth_pcr <- min(sample_sums(ps_pcr))
hill_pcr_raw  <- hill_inext_size(ps_pcr, level = rar_depth_pcr, label = "Per-PCR-replicate")

m_pcr  <- otu_mat_of(ps_pcr)
md_pcr <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps_pcr))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(m_pcr), rownames(md_pcr)))
md_pcr$Season <- factor(md_pcr$Season, levels = c("winter", "summer"))
md_pcr$Year   <- factor(md_pcr$Year)
md_pcr <- add_indivID_glm(md_pcr)
# Groups the (up to) 2 technical replicates of the same dung sample.
md_pcr$pcr_replicate_id <- droplevels(factor(md_pcr$sample))

hill_pcr <- data.frame(
  pcr_row = rownames(m_pcr),
  q0 = hill_pcr_raw$q0,
  q1 = hill_pcr_raw$q1,
  q2 = hill_pcr_raw$q2,
  Season = md_pcr$Season, Year = md_pcr$Year,
  indivID_glm = md_pcr$indivID_glm,
  pcr_replicate_id = md_pcr$pcr_replicate_id, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
write.csv(hill_pcr, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_hill_per_pcr_replicate.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

hl_pcr <- hill_pcr %>% pivot_longer(c(q0, q1, q2), names_to = "q", values_to = "value")
p_hill_box <- ggplot(hl_pcr, aes(Season, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = Year), width = 0.15, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~q, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = as_labeller(c(q0 = "q0 richness", q1 = "q1 Shannon",
                                      q2 = "q2 Simpson"))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Per-PCR-replicate Hill diversity (iNEXT3D, size-standardised to %d reads)",
                       rar_depth_pcr), y = "Hill number", x = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
save_png(p_hill_box, "H2_hill_boxplot_Season_pcr.png", width = 10, height = 4.5)

# Fallback ladder if the full random-effects structure is singular: drop
# (1|indivID_glm) first (many NA-individual singleton placeholders), then
# (1|Year), then plain lm(). (1|pcr_replicate_id) is kept as long as possible.
# Whichever structure converged is reported in `re_structure`.
fit_h2_lmm <- function(dat, qcol) {
  ladder <- list(
    "Season + (1|Year) + (1|indivID_glm) + (1|pcr_replicate_id)",
    "Season + (1|Year) + (1|pcr_replicate_id)",
    "Season + (1|pcr_replicate_id)")
  fit <- NULL; re_structure <- NA_character_
  for (rhs in ladder) {
    fit <- tryCatch(lmerTest::lmer(as.formula(paste(qcol, "~", rhs)), data = dat),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    re_structure <- rhs
    if (!is.null(fit) && !lme4::isSingular(fit)) break
  }
  if (is.null(fit) || lme4::isSingular(fit)) {
    fit <- lm(as.formula(paste(qcol, "~ Season")), data = dat)
    re_structure <- "Season (lm, no random effects)"
  }
  co  <- summary(fit)$coefficients
  est <- co["Seasonsummer", "Estimate"]; se <- co["Seasonsummer", "Std. Error"]
  pv  <- if ("Pr(>|t|)" %in% colnames(co)) co["Seasonsummer", "Pr(>|t|)"]
         else co["Seasonsummer", "Pr(>|z|)"]
  data.frame(metric = qcol, re_structure = re_structure,
             summer_minus_winter = round(est, 3),
             lwr = round(est - 1.96 * se, 3), upr = round(est + 1.96 * se, 3),
             p = round(pv, 4))
}
write.csv(dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), function(q) fit_h2_lmm(hill_pcr, q))),
          file.path(tab_dir, "H2_lmm_season_effect.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Figure S8 -- per-sample Hill diversity (PCR-collapsed, size-standardised)
# ===========================================================================
# Raw counts (alldat$nopool): iNEXT.3D does the standardisation itself, to the
# same depth alldat.rfy was rarefied to. Deterministic, no seed. This is the
# PER-SAMPLE level (n = 52), deliberately distinct from the PCR-replicate level
# of Table S9c above.
ps_rar_sample <- alldat$nopool
m_rar_sample  <- otu_mat_of(ps_rar_sample)
md_rar_sample <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps_rar_sample))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(m_rar_sample), rownames(md_rar_sample)))
md_rar_sample$Season <- factor(md_rar_sample$Season, levels = c("winter", "summer"))
md_rar_sample$Year   <- factor(md_rar_sample$Year)
md_rar_sample <- add_indivID_glm(md_rar_sample)

samp_depth      <- min(rowSums(m_rar_sample))
hill_sample_raw <- hill_inext_size(ps_rar_sample, level = samp_depth, label = "Per-sample")

hill_sample <- data.frame(
  sample = rownames(m_rar_sample),
  q0 = hill_sample_raw$q0,
  q1 = hill_sample_raw$q1,
  q2 = hill_sample_raw$q2,
  Season = md_rar_sample$Season, Year = md_rar_sample$Year,
  indivID_glm = md_rar_sample$indivID_glm, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
write.csv(hill_sample, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_hill_per_sample.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

hl_sample <- hill_sample %>% pivot_longer(c(q0, q1, q2), names_to = "q", values_to = "value")
p_hill_sample_box <- ggplot(hl_sample, aes(Season, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = Year), width = 0.15, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~q, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = as_labeller(c(q0 = "q0 richness", q1 = "q1 Shannon",
                                      q2 = "q2 Simpson"))) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Per-sample Hill diversity (PCR-collapsed, iNEXT3D size-standardised to %d reads)",
                       samp_depth), y = "Hill number", x = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
save_png(p_hill_sample_box, "H2_hill_boxplot_Season.png", width = 10, height = 4.5)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S9 (primary) + S9b -- Season effect on PER-SAMPLE Hill numbers
# ===========================================================================
# The test is fitted on the same unit Figure S8 / Fig. 4B plot: one value per
# dung sample (n = 52), size-standardised above. Year is a FIXED effect (three
# levels is too few to estimate a variance -- the replicate-level fits above went
# singular on it). Individual bird is not modelled: only 3 birds were sampled
# more than once. Primary family: gamma with a log link (Hill numbers are
# positive and right-skewed; exp(coef) is a summer/winter ratio). Season x Year is
# tested by F-test and dAICc against the additive model. Table S9b repeats the
# Season test under other families, as the Paramo revision did, because the q0
# result is the one sensitive to that choice.
aicc <- function(m) { k <- length(coef(m)) + 1L; n <- nobs(m)
  AIC(m) + 2 * k * (k + 1) / (n - k - 1) }
hs <- hill_sample; hs$Season <- factor(hs$Season, levels = c("winter", "summer"))
s9 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), function(q) {
  f_add <- as.formula(paste(q, "~ Season + Year"))
  f_int <- as.formula(paste(q, "~ Season * Year"))
  g_add <- glm(f_add, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = hs)
  g_int <- glm(f_int, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = hs)
  dr  <- drop1(g_add, test = "F")
  ci  <- exp(confint.default(g_add)["Seasonsummer", ])
  data.frame(metric = q, n = nobs(g_add),
             mean_winter = mean(hs[[q]][hs$Season == "winter"]),
             mean_summer = mean(hs[[q]][hs$Season == "summer"]),
             ratio_summer_winter = exp(coef(g_add)[["Seasonsummer"]]),
             ratio_lwr = ci[[1]], ratio_upr = ci[[2]],
             F_season = dr["Season", "F value"], p_season = dr["Season", "Pr(>F)"],
             p_year = dr["Year", "Pr(>F)"],
             p_season_x_year = anova(g_add, g_int, test = "F")[2, "Pr(>F)"],
             dAICc_interaction = aicc(g_int) - aicc(g_add),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
write.csv(s9, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_season_effect_per_sample.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

s9b <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("q0", "q1", "q2"), function(q) {
  f  <- as.formula(paste(q, "~ Season + Year"))
  fl <- as.formula(paste("log(", q, ") ~ Season + Year"))
  g  <- glm(f, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = hs)
  la <- lm(f, data = hs); ll <- lm(fl, data = hs)
  data.frame(metric = q,
             p_gaussian  = drop1(la, test = "F")["Season", "Pr(>F)"],
             p_lognormal = drop1(ll, test = "F")["Season", "Pr(>F)"],
             p_gamma     = drop1(g,  test = "F")["Season", "Pr(>F)"],
             p_wilcoxon  = wilcox.test(as.formula(paste(q, "~ Season")), data = hs)$p.value,
             # AIC on the response scale; the log-normal gets the Jacobian term
             # so it is comparable (the Paramo family screen omitted it).
             AIC_gaussian  = AIC(la),
             AIC_lognormal = AIC(ll) + 2 * sum(log(hs[[q]])),
             AIC_gamma     = AIC(g),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
write.csv(s9b, file.path(tab_dir, "H2_season_effect_family_sensitivity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S10 -- dominance and evenness, per sample
# ===========================================================================
ps <- alldat$nopool
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix")
if (!taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)      # taxa x samples
sd <- as.data.frame(sample_data(ps))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(otu_mat), rownames(sd)))
rel_mat <- sweep(otu_mat, 2, colSums(otu_mat), "/")

pielou_J <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; (-sum(p * log(p))) / log(length(p)) }

# Richness is the SIZE-STANDARDISED q0 of Figure S8 (12,615 reads), not the raw
# OTU count: summer libraries are ~2.6x deeper, so raw counts compare unequal
# effort. The raw count is kept in the per-sample CSV for reference only.
# Pielou J stays on the raw counts: checked against the size-standardised
# evenness ln(q1)/ln(q0), r = 0.995 across samples and the same seasonal contrast
# (0.41 vs 0.75, Wilcoxon p ~ 1e-7), so depth does not drive it.
hs_i <- match(colnames(otu_mat), hill_sample$sample); stopifnot(!anyNA(hs_i))
dom_df <- data.frame(
  sample = colnames(otu_mat), Season = sd$Season, Year = sd$Year,
  richness  = hill_sample$q0[hs_i],
  richness_observed_raw = colSums(otu_mat > 0),
  top1_prop = apply(rel_mat, 2, max),
  pielou_J  = apply(rel_mat, 2, pielou_J),
  evenness_size_std = log(hill_sample$q1[hs_i]) / log(hill_sample$q0[hs_i]),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

season_summary <- dom_df %>% group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_richness      = round(mean(richness), 1),
            mean_top1_prop_pct = round(100 * mean(top1_prop), 1),
            mean_pielou_J      = round(mean(pielou_J), 2), .groups = "drop")

wilcox_rich <- wilcox.test(richness  ~ Season, data = dom_df)
wilcox_top1 <- wilcox.test(top1_prop ~ Season, data = dom_df)
wilcox_J    <- wilcox.test(pielou_J  ~ Season, data = dom_df)

write.csv(dom_df, file.path(tab_dir, "report_dominance_per_sample.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(season_summary %>%
            mutate(wilcox_p_richness  = round(wilcox_rich$p.value, 5),
                   wilcox_p_top1_prop = round(wilcox_top1$p.value, 5),
                   wilcox_p_pielou_J  = round(wilcox_J$p.value, 5)),
          file.path(tab_dir, "report_dominance_summary.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S11 -- top-5 dominant OTUs per Season
# ===========================================================================
tax <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
seasons <- levels(factor(sd$Season))
top5_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seasons, function(s) {
  shares   <- rowMeans(rel_mat[, rownames(sd)[sd$Season == s], drop = FALSE])
  top5_ids <- names(sort(shares, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
  data.frame(Season = s, OTU = top5_ids,
             mean_pct_share = round(100 * shares[top5_ids], 2),
             tax[top5_ids, c("Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species")],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
write.csv(top5_df, file.path(tab_dir, "report_top5_otu_by_season.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# ===========================================================================
# Table S3 (Section 3.2, E2) -- coprophilous-genus screen
# ===========================================================================
# ONE list, used for both Table S3 and the Season test below. It is the
# standard palynological coprophilous set extended with the four dung-
# associated genera that actually carry the seasonal signal in this dataset:
# Thelebolus, Coniochaeta, Psathyrella and Stropharia (Sections 5.4, 6.2, 8.2).
# Sections 8 and 9 apply a 14-genus variant of this list to the FUNGuild guild
# rule (it omits Sporormia, Psathyrella and Stropharia); see 8_functional_guilds.R.
COPRO_GENERA <- c("Sordaria", "Podospora", "Cercophora", "Chaetomium",
                  "Schizothecium", "Preussia", "Sporormiella", "Delitschia",
                  "Pilobolus", "Ascobolus", "Coprinopsis", "Saccobolus", "Sporormia",
                  "Thelebolus", "Coniochaeta", "Psathyrella", "Stropharia")

# UNITE taxonomy carries rank prefixes ("g__Thelebolus"); strip them or the
# %in% match silently fails. "unidentified" placeholders become NA.
strip_pref <- function(x) {
  x <- ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_, sub("^[a-z]__", "", x))
  x[x == "" | grepl("unidentified", x, ignore.case = TRUE)] <- NA
  x
}
genus_clean <- strip_pref(tax$Genus)
copro_flag  <- !is.na(genus_clean) & genus_clean %in% COPRO_GENERA
copro_otus  <- rownames(tax)[copro_flag]

w <- sd$Season == "winter"; s <- sd$Season == "summer"
copro_by_otu <- data.frame(
  OTU     = copro_otus,
  Genus   = genus_clean[copro_flag],
  Species = strip_pref(tax$Species[copro_flag]),
  winter_mean_pct = round(100 * rowMeans(rel_mat[copro_otus, w, drop = FALSE]), 3),
  summer_mean_pct = round(100 * rowMeans(rel_mat[copro_otus, s, drop = FALSE]), 3),
  occ_winter = rowSums(rel_mat[copro_otus, w, drop = FALSE] > 0),
  occ_summer = rowSums(rel_mat[copro_otus, s, drop = FALSE] > 0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
copro_by_otu <- copro_by_otu[order(-(copro_by_otu$winter_mean_pct +
                                     copro_by_otu$summer_mean_pct)), ]
write.csv(copro_by_otu, file.path(tab_dir, "report_coprophilous_by_season_v2.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# Per-sample total coprophilous read share, and the Season test quoted in
# Section 3.2 -- same COPRO_GENERA list as Table S3 above.
copro_df <- data.frame(sample = colnames(rel_mat), Season = sd$Season,
                       copro_pct_share = 100 * colSums(rel_mat[copro_otus, , drop = FALSE]))
print(copro_df %>% group_by(Season) %>%
        summarise(mean_pct = round(mean(copro_pct_share), 2),
                  median_pct = round(median(copro_pct_share), 2), .groups = "drop"))
print(wilcox.test(copro_pct_share ~ Season, data = copro_df))
```

#### Documentation notes — Section 5 {.unnumbered}

This dark, winter-associated OTU is an **E1** dark taxon (Section 3.4) — and, being winter-persistent, a candidate to carry into the deferred H3 plant-covariation analysis downstream — and it revises the original "stable cold-adapted *Thelebolus*–*Sporormiella* core" framing: those recognizable coprophilous genera are part of the summer-inflated, activity-tracking tail, not a season-independent core.
:::

## Section 6: Lineage-specific seasonal responses — GLLVM (H1, OTU-resolved) {.page-break-before}

Sections 4 and 5 establish that the community shifts between seasons (H1) and that summer samples gain a long rare tail while becoming more dominance-skewed (H2). This section resolves H1 to the level of individual OTUs. We fit a generalized linear latent-variable model (GLLVM, negative-binomial) of per-OTU counts as a function of Season (winter as reference), with a library-size offset and random intercepts for individual bird and PCR replicate; the model is fitted on the full-complexity, one-row-per-PCR-replicate object (`Scripts/7_gllvm.R`, objects `models/fit_nb_2.rds` and `models/fit_nb_2_2.rds`). It answers which lineages drive the turnover — each with its own model uncertainty — and, through its latent variables, describes the residual co-occurrence that remains after Season is accounted for.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
<!-- SEE NOTE: a real scientific limitation, not a status note — you may want one plain sentence of this to survive into the submitted version -->

::: callout-warning
**Fitted on the pre-depth-fix object.** These fits were built on the full-complexity object as it stood *before* the July depth-filter correction: 57 samples (114 PCR-replicate rows) and 327 filtered OTUs, versus the 52-sample / 278-OTU canonical object used everywhere else in this appendix. The library-size offset, per-OTU abundance weights, and the Poisson baseline in Table S-GLLVMa are all reconstructed from that same pre-fix object so the section is internally consistent. The five extra samples and larger OTU set do not change the direction or rank of any result below, but exact coefficients will move slightly when the models are refitted on the corrected object — treat the numbers as robust in sign and rank, provisional in the last digit.
:::
:::

::: callout-warning
**Read the per-OTU coefficients in this section as signs and ranks, not effect sizes.** Two limitations apply (added 2026-09-29; wording to be finalised). (i) The models were fitted on the pre-depth-filter-correction object (57 samples, 114 replicate rows, 327 OTUs), not the canonical 52-sample object used elsewhere. (ii) Many Season coefficients are not estimable as finite effects: OTUs absent or nearly absent from one season push an unpooled fixed coefficient toward ±∞. 134 of the 327 OTUs are flagged for this (`separation`), and 101 of the 209 OTUs counted as significant are among them (the largest reaching β ≈ 1,295 on the log scale). Among the 193 unflagged OTUs, 106 still have \|β\| \> 10, i.e. implausible fold changes (e¹⁰ ≈ 22,000), including the *Sporormiella* and *Coniochaeta* values quoted below (β ≈ 17). The OTU-level seasonal pattern is carried by HMSC in Section 9, which is fitted on the current data with shrinkage.
:::

### 6.1 Model choice

```{r tab-gllvm-aic}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_model_comparison.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mc$logLik <- signif(mc$logLik, 4); mc$AIC <- signif(mc$AIC, 5); mc$dAIC <- signif(mc$dAIC, 4)
kable(mc[, c("model", "logLik", "AIC", "dAIC")],
      col.names = c("Model", "logLik", "AIC", "ΔAIC"),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMa. GLLVM model comparison on the same 327-OTU / 114-row response matrix. The negative-binomial fits are dramatically better than the Poisson baseline (strong overdispersion), and two latent variables are preferred over one (ΔAIC ≈ 723). fit_nb_2_2 is the reported model.")
```

The negative-binomial family is strongly favoured over Poisson (the Poisson log-likelihood is worse by \~5 orders of magnitude, the signature of severe count overdispersion), and two latent variables outperform one by ΔAIC ≈ 723. We therefore report `fit_nb_2_2` (negative-binomial, two latent variables).

### 6.2 Which OTUs drive the seasonal turnover

For every OTU we extract the Season coefficient (β on the GLLVM log scale; positive = higher in summer) together with the model's own Wald 95% CI, and flag significance at a Benjamini–Hochberg FDR of 5%.

![](figures/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMa**: Season response of the 30 most abundant OTUs, each with its model 95% CI, coloured by Order; filled points are significant at BH q \< 0.05. Of the 327 modelled OTUs, 209 are significant, and the turnover is strongly asymmetric: 166 OTUs are enriched in summer versus 43 in winter. A further 134 OTUs are near-complete "on/off" seasonal switches (essentially absent in one season); these have real but non-interpretable point estimates (β in the hundreds, or exploding CIs) and are flagged (`separation`) and excluded both from this panel and from Table S-GLLVMb, which reports only well-estimated OTUs; they are retained in the full per-OTU table (`tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv`).

```{r tab-gllvm-otu}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
oc  <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
well <- oc %>% filter(!separation, sig)
fmt <- function(df) df %>% transmute(OTU = taxon, Genus, Order,
                                     beta = round(beta_season, 2),
                                     `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
                                     `BH q` = signif(p_adj, 2))
kable(well %>% arrange(desc(beta_season)) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>% fmt(),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMb(i). Most strongly summer-enriched well-estimated OTUs (BH q < 0.05).")
kable(well %>% arrange(beta_season) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>% fmt(),
      caption = "Table S-GLLVMb(ii). Most strongly winter-enriched well-estimated OTUs (BH q < 0.05). Full per-OTU table: tables/gllvm_perOTU_season_coef.csv.")
```

Two results connect directly to the dominance analysis (Section 5.4). The coprophilous taxa that dominate summer read share behave differently under the model: OTU636 (*Sporormiella*, β ≈ 17.2) and OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*, β ≈ 17.3) are both significantly summer-enriched, but OTU1 (*Thelebolus*, β ≈ 3.0) is not significant (95% CI crosses zero) — its large summer read share is carried by a few samples and high among-individual variance rather than a model-robust per-OTU shift. On the winter side, the dark taxon OTU1369 (class Dothideomycetes) is significantly winter-enriched (β ≈ −6.9): the GLLVM independently corroborates the dominance/E1 finding that winter's persistent OTU is a taxonomically unresolved lineage.

Aggregating to genus gives the broader pattern:

![](figures/panel_AB_heatmap_barplot_season.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMc**: Genus-level seasonal response. (A) Heatmap of the abundance-weighted mean β per genus; (B) the same as a point-range plot with bootstrapped 95% CIs. Warm = summer-enriched, cool = winter-enriched.

```{r tab-gllvm-genus}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
gt <- read.csv("tables/genus_table_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt %>% transmute(Order, Genus, n_OTUs,
                 `total reads` = round(total_w_abund),
                 `median beta` = round(median_beta_season, 1),
                 `weighted-mean beta` = round(w_mean_beta_season, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(`weighted-mean beta`)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table S-GLLVMc. Genus-level seasonal responses (β = summer vs winter, GLLVM log scale) for genera passing the abundance/effect-size thresholds. Full detail in models/genus_table_season.csv.")
```

### 6.3 Residual co-occurrence beyond Season

![](figures/gllvm_residual_ordination.png)

**Figure S-GLLVMb**: Model-based ordination on the two latent variables of `fit_nb_2_2` — the residual OTU co-occurrence structure that remains *after* Season and the random effects are accounted for. Sites are coloured by Season; the eight strongest species loadings are labelled. This is the model-based counterpart to the unconstrained robust-Aitchison PCoA in Section 4.1: because Season is already in the model as a fixed effect, the two seasons overlap substantially here, confirming that Season captures a coherent axis of the community rather than all of its covariation. A small set of winter sites separates along the second latent variable (winter scores are \~3.4× as variable as summer ones on that axis, Fligner–Killeen p = 0.013; seven of the eight most extreme sites are winter). This is specific to that axis and is not a statement about which season is more heterogeneous overall — on the first latent variable summer is the more variable season, and Section 4.2 finds summer significantly the more dispersed in total composition (mean distance to centroid 24.8 versus 13.6, p = 0.002).

## Section 7: Diet-tracking and Bayesian models — H2 and H3 {.page-break-before}

### 7.1 Diet richness and fungal diversity — Bayesian mechanism (H2)

Section 5 established the coarse prediction of H2: summer communities are richer than winter ones, in step with the richer summer diet. Here we test the finer mechanism directly, on the subset of samples for which we have paired plant ITS2 diet data (**n = 27** dung samples): does an individual sample's fungal diversity track the richness of its own dietary plant community? Fungal Hill diversity is modelled as a function of standardised plant (diet) richness, adjusting for Season, in a Bayesian Gamma regression with a log link (brms). H2's mechanism is supported if the plant-richness slope is positive with posterior probability P(slope \> 0) \> 0.95.

The preregistration specified Year and individual bird as random intercepts. At this matched sample size that structure is unidentifiable — the 27 samples come from 24 distinct birds, so an individual random effect cannot be separated from residual variation, and Year spans only three levels — and the random-effects model does not converge. We therefore report two complementary, cleanly-converged fixed-effect models that bracket the estimate: a **Season-adjusted** model (`plant_richness + Season + Year`, Year as a fixed effect) and a more parsimonious **drop-Year** model (`plant_richness + Season`). Both model the raw Hill number with a Gamma likelihood and log link, the same family as the per-sample Season test of Table S9, with a weakly-informative prior on the slope (Normal(0, 1) per standard deviation of plant richness, on the log scale).

![](figures/H2_diet_richness_fit.png)

**Figure S9**: Per-sample fungal Hill q1 diversity against rarefied dietary plant richness (n = 27 matched samples), coloured by Season. Both Gamma (log link) model fits are shown — Season-adjusted (solid) and drop-Year (dashed) — with the 95% credible ribbon for the primary Season-adjusted model. Fitted lines are drawn at the reference Season/Year; the quantity of interest is the common positive slope.

```{r tab-h2mech-compare}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_model_comparison.csv", check.names = FALSE)
mc_disp <- data.frame(
  Model       = mc$model,
  Structure   = mc$formula,
  `Slope (median, log scale)` = round(mc$median, 3),
  `95% CrI`   = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", mc$lwr95, mc$upr95),
  `Ratio per SD` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(mc$median)),
  `P(slope>0)`= round(mc$P_gt0, 3),
  Divergences = mc$divergences,
  `Clears 0.95?` = ifelse(mc$supported, "yes", "no"),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(mc_disp,
      caption = "Table S12. H2-mechanism: the two complementary Bayesian Gamma (log link) models of fungal Hill q1 diversity vs. dietary plant richness. Slopes are on the log scale per standard deviation of plant richness; 'Ratio per SD' = exp(median slope), the multiplicative change in fungal Hill q1. Both converge cleanly (0 divergences, Rhat < 1.01) and place the diet-richness slope positive.")
```

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
```{r tab-h2mech-family}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
fc <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_family_choice.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Family      = fc$family,
  Model       = fc$model,
  `Slope (median)` = sprintf("%.3f (%s)", fc$median, fc$slope_scale),
  `95% CrI`   = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", fc$lwr95, fc$upr95),
  `P(slope>0)`= round(fc$P_gt0, 3),
  `PPC skewness p` = round(fc$ppc_p_skewness, 3),
  `ΔELPD vs primary (SE)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", fc$elpd_diff_vs_primary, fc$se_diff),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S12b (documentation build). Family choice for the H2-mechanism model. Until 2026-09 the model was Gaussian on the z-scored Hill number; it fails the posterior-predictive skewness check (Bayesian p ≈ 0) and is outperformed by ≈ 13 ELPD (PSIS-LOO on the raw q1 scale). Gamma and lognormal fit equally well; Gamma was adopted because Table S9 already uses it. Source: 6_diversity_analyses.R Section 3b; pilot comparison of further families in brms_refit/MEMO_brms_refit.md.")
```
::::

Both models place the diet-richness slope firmly positive (medians +0.22 and +0.34 on the log scale, i.e. fungal Hill q1 multiplied by 1.24 and 1.40 per standard deviation of plant richness), with posterior support of **P(slope \> 0) = 0.91** (Season-adjusted) and **0.99** (drop-Year). The drop-Year model clears the preregistered 0.95 threshold; the Season-adjusted model sits just below it. The direction of the effect is therefore consistent, and the weight of posterior evidence favours the predicted positive diet-richness → fungal-diversity relationship.

![](figures/H2_mechanism_slope_posterior.png)

**Figure S10**: Posterior distribution of the diet-richness slope (log scale, per standard deviation of plant richness) for both Gamma models. The mass of both posteriors lies to the right of zero (dashed line).

The signal is consistent across the choice of Hill order: refitting with richness (q0) and Simpson-equivalent (q2) diversity as the outcome gives positive slopes throughout, with P(slope \> 0) between 0.78 and 0.99 (Table S13). No specification reverses the direction.

```{r tab-h2mech-sens}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sn <- read.csv("tables/H2_mechanism_sensitivity.csv", check.names = FALSE)
sn_disp <- data.frame(
  `Hill order` = sn$metric,
  Model        = sn$model,
  `Slope (median)` = round(sn$median, 3),
  `95% CrI`    = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", sn$lwr95, sn$upr95),
  `P(slope>0)` = round(sn$P_gt0, 3),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(sn_disp,
      caption = "Table S13. Sensitivity of the diet-richness slope to Hill order (q0 richness, q1 Shannon, q2 Simpson) under both model structures, each a Gamma (log link) model of the raw Hill number; slopes on the log scale per SD of plant richness. All six estimates are positive.")
```

<!-- DANIEL (exp/brms-refit, 2026-10-01): numbers above are updated to the Gamma models; the interpretive
prose below is untouched and yours to rewrite. Two points from the refit bear on it: (1) "primarily at the
seasonal scale" is backwards — Season is in both models, so the slope IS within-season, and the
between-season contrast runs the other way (2026-09-10 Hill-order memo); (2) under every family tried,
removing S_1_7_P1_8E takes P(slope > 0) to ~0.5 (Table S14 most-influential sample). -->

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
**Ecological interpretation.** Dietary plant richness is markedly higher in summer than winter, so most of the diet–diversity relationship is expressed through the *seasonal* contrast — which is exactly the diet-driven mechanism H2 proposes: the seasonal diet shift is the dominant axis of variation in propagule supply, and summer's richer plant intake is accompanied by a richer fungal community. Within a single season the diet-richness gradient is short (only a few plant OTUs separate one sample from another), so the per-sample effect is correspondingly modest.

Consistent with a modest, gradient-limited signal at this sample size, the estimate is carried by the samples at the extremes of the diet-richness range: a single leave-one-out omission moves the slope within the ranges in Table S14, and rank (Spearman) correlations within each Season are close to zero — the parametric slope reflects the between-season spread of the gradient more than fine within-season covariation. The honest reading is therefore a **weak, directionally-consistent signal**: fungal diversity does tend to rise with dietary plant richness, primarily at the seasonal scale, but the per-sample effect is not resolved decisively at n = 27 and is a clear target for a larger diet-matched sample.
:::

```{r tab-h2mech-robust}
names(rb) <- c("Check", "Group", "Quantity", "Value")
kable(rb,
      caption = "Table S14. Robustness of the diet-richness slope: leave-one-out influence (slope of the equivalent frequentist Gamma GLM on the log scale, its range across single-sample omissions, and the most influential sample) and Spearman rank correlations overall and within each Season. The Spearman rows are unadjusted marginal correlations; the leave-one-out rows are Season/Year-adjusted, so the two need not agree in sign.")
```

### 7.2 OTU–plant covariation (H3) - H3 not supported - still working 

Section 7.1 asked whether overall fungal diversity tracks overall diet richness. H3 is finer-grained and taxon-resolved: does each fungal OTU covary with particular diet-plant taxa, and — the preregistered contrast — do recognised coprophilous taxa show the diffuse, non-specific plant associations expected of dung specialists dispersed independently of any host plant, while other taxa may show the tight, single-plant covariation that would flag a likely ingested endophyte passenger? Inference is strictly forward-directional: a tight single-plant association is read as evidence of a likely ingested passenger; a diffuse or absent association is not read as evidence of gut/dung residency.

**Model.** We fit a single hierarchical joint negative-binomial model (brms) to the diet-matched subset. To retain as many matched samples as possible we use the PCR-replicate-level, minimally depth-filtered object (mirroring the GLLVM of Section 6) rather than the collapsed, 10,000-read-filtered object of Sections 4–5; this recovers three additional low-depth winter dung samples that carry paired plant data, raising the matched subset to **n = 30 biological samples (60 PCR-replicate libraries; 19 winter, 11 summer)**. Each fungal OTU count is modelled with a per-replicate log-library-size offset (so shallow libraries are accommodated, not discarded), the six dominant diet-plant genera (rCLR-transformed, standardised) as predictors, Season and Year as population-level covariates, per-OTU varying intercepts and plant slopes (the partial-pooling "joint model"), and a per-OTU biological-sample random effect so the two PCR replicates of a sample are treated as replication rather than independent samples. This substitutes a sample random effect for the preregistered "individual" one (unidentifiable here — nearly every sample is a distinct bird), for the same reason as Section 7.1. Forty-six OTUs present in ≥5 of the 30 samples are modelled. For each OTU we summarise the specificity of its plant coefficients with a Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) of the \|plant slopes\| — ≈1/6 = 0.17 if covariation is spread evenly across all six genera, up to 1 if concentrated on a single plant — and flag a resolved single-plant association when the 90% credible interval of the OTU's strongest plant slope excludes zero. The preregistered contrast compares specificity between FUNGuild-flagged coprophilous OTUs and plant-associated (endophyte/phyllosphere/plant-saprotroph) OTUs. The model converged cleanly (maximum R̂ = 1.004, no divergent transitions).

![](figures/H3_perOTU_plant_coef.png)

**Figure S11**: Posterior-median covariation of each modelled fungal OTU (rows, ordered by specificity and grouped by FUNGuild guild class) with each dominant diet-plant genus (columns), on the log (negative-binomial) scale; red = positive, blue = negative. The three recognised coprophilous taxa (*Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta*, *Sporormiella*) covary *positively* and strongly with *Vaccinium*, whereas most other OTUs covary negatively with it.

```{r tab-h3-spec}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
si <- read.csv("tables/H3_specificity_index.csv", check.names = FALSE)
si_disp <- head(si, 12)
kable(data.frame(
  OTU            = si_disp$OTU_ID,
  Genus          = ifelse(is.na(si_disp$Genus), "—", si_disp$Genus),
  `Prev. (/30)`  = si_disp$prevalence,
  Specificity    = round(si_disp$specificity_HHI, 2),
  `Top plant`    = si_disp$dominant_plant,
  `Top slope [90% CrI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", si_disp$dom_slope_med,
                                  si_disp$dom_slope_lwr90, si_disp$dom_slope_upr90),
  Resolved       = ifelse(si_disp$resolved_single_plant, "yes", "—"),
  Guild          = si_disp$guild_group,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S15. The twelve most plant-specific fungal OTUs (of 46 modelled), ranked by the Herfindahl specificity of their plant coefficients. Only OTU1 (Thelebolus) reaches a resolved single-plant association (its Vaccinium slope's 90% CrI excludes zero). Diffuse baseline (six genera) = 0.17.")
```

**Result.** For almost every OTU the plant covariation is too weak to resolve at this sample size: of the 46 OTUs, **only one — OTU1 (*Thelebolus*) — shows a resolved single-plant association** (a strong positive *Vaccinium* slope, median +2.30 on the log scale, 90% CrI \[0.18, 4.62\]). This single tight association runs *opposite* to the preregistered expectation: *Thelebolus* is a recognised coprophilous dung specialist, not a phyllosphere/endophyte passenger. More generally, the three coprophilous taxa are the *most* plant-concentrated OTUs in the dataset, not the least (Figure S12): the coprophilous group has a higher median specificity than the plant-associated group (0.38 vs 0.30) — the reverse of the predicted "coprophilous = more diffuse" pattern. The contrast is not supported in either direction under uncertainty: a one-sided Wilcoxon test of the preregistered direction gives p = 0.72, and propagating the full posterior, P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.36. The genus-list sensitivity grouping (coprophilous = *Thelebolus*/*Sporormiella*/*Coniochaeta*) tells the same story (0.51 vs 0.30).

![](figures/H3_specificity_contrast.png)

**Figure S12**: Per-OTU plant-association specificity (Herfindahl index) by FUNGuild guild class. Contrary to the preregistered prediction, coprophilous OTUs are if anything *more* plant-concentrated than plant-associated ones. Dashed line = maximally-diffuse baseline (1/6).

```{r tab-h3-contrast}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
ct <- read.csv("tables/H3_specificity_contrast.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Grouping                    = ct$grouping,
  `n copro`                   = ct$n_coprophilous,
  `n plant-assoc`             = ct$n_plant_assoc,
  `Copro HHI`                 = round(ct$copro_spec_med, 2),
  `Plant-assoc HHI`           = round(ct$plant_spec_med, 2),
  `Wilcoxon p (copro<plant)`  = round(ct$wilcox_p_copro_lower, 2),
  `P(copro more diffuse)`     = round(ct$P_copro_lower, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S16. Preregistered coprophilous-vs-plant-associated specificity contrast (FUNGuild primary grouping; COPRO_GENERA genus list as sensitivity). Neither grouping supports the predicted 'coprophilous more diffuse' direction. The full per-OTU × plant coefficient table is provided as tables/H3_perOTU_plant_coef.csv (Table S17).")
```

**Interpretation.** H3, as preregistered, is **not supported**: taxonomically recognised coprophilous taxa do *not* show more diffuse plant associations than other taxa — if anything the reverse. The single interpretable plant signal is a *Vaccinium*–*Thelebolus* covariation, and its ecology is the opposite of the "ingested passenger" reading H3 was built to detect: *Thelebolus* is a dung specialist, and *Vaccinium* (with *Empetrum*) is the winter browse of ptarmigan at this site. Because Season is already a covariate this is a within-season-adjusted association, but the residual gradient is short; the most parsimonious reading is that the winter-browse plants and the persistent dung-fungal core co-vary as parallel seasonal signatures of the same samples, not that *Thelebolus* is carried into the gut on *Vaccinium* tissue. This dovetails with Section 6, where *Thelebolus* (OTU1) was the one coprophile *without* a clean seasonal differential-abundance signal, and with the E2 documentation in Section 3.2.

**Limitation.** Even at n = 30 the diet is dominated by a few plant genera (*Betula* near-ubiquitous, then *Vaccinium*/*Empetrum*), so specificity can be assessed over only \~6 genera and the coprophilous group is small (6 OTUs). We therefore report H3 as a directional, exploratory result rather than a decisive test — and, consistent with the forward-directional inference rule, the absence of tight single-plant passenger signatures is **not** evidence that the dung mycobiome is gut-resident. A larger, more diet-even matched sample is the necessary next step.

### 7.3 OTU–plant covariation — GLLVM cross-check (H3)

To check that the H3 verdict of Section 7.2 is not an artefact of one modelling framework, we repeat the analysis with a generalised linear latent-variable model (GLLVM) — the same model-based framework used for the OTU-resolved H1 in Section 6, now with the diet-plant predictors added. Everything about the data is held identical to the Bayesian model: the same PCR-replicate-level matched subset (**n = 30 biological samples, 60 libraries; 46 OTUs present in ≥5 samples**), the same six standardised diet-plant genera (rCLR-transformed), the same per-library log-size offset, and the same specificity index and preregistered coprophilous-vs-plant-associated contrast. Only the estimator differs, which is the point: agreement across two very different fitting machineries is stronger evidence than either alone.

**Model.** Each OTU's counts are modelled with a negative-binomial GLLVM (`gllvm`), with Season and Year as community covariates, a per-OTU (species-specific) *fixed* slope for each plant genus, a biological-sample random row effect (so the two PCR replicates of a sample count as replication, not independent samples), and the log-library-size offset. We fit 0, 1 and 2 residual latent variables and select by AIC; here **num.lv = 0** is preferred — beyond the sample random effect the latent variables capture no further residual co-occurrence (so, unlike Section 6, there is no residual ordination to show). One difference from the Bayesian model is forced by the software: the natural partial-pooling analog (`gllvm`'s `randomX` species-specific *random* slopes) is silently dropped on this dataset, returning no plant-slope parameters at all. We therefore estimate the plant slopes as *fixed* per-OTU coefficients with Wald standard errors — an **unpooled** frequentist estimate that brackets the Bayesian *pooled* one from the other side. Rare on/off OTUs push their fixed coefficients toward ±∞ (near-separation); as in Section 6 these are flagged (16 of 46 OTUs) and excluded from the specificity ranking, contrast and plots, leaving **30 well-estimated OTUs**. Specificity is the same Herfindahl index of the \|plant slopes\|; a *resolved single-plant association* here means the 90 % Wald interval of an OTU's strongest plant slope excludes zero.

::: callout-warning
**Caveat on the per-OTU slopes (added 2026-09-29; wording to be finalised).** Even among the 30 retained OTUs the unpooled slopes are large for a per-SD predictor (median \|slope\| 1.9, 90th percentile 7.0, maximum 15.9 on the log scale), so the count of Wald-resolved associations in this section overstates what is estimable; the Bayesian pooled model of Section 7.2 resolves only 1 of 46. The verdict this section supports is the model-level one — AIC prefers the plant-free model and the coprophilous-versus-plant-associated contrast is not significant — not the individual slopes.
:::

```{r tab-h3g-aic}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
mc <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_model_comparison.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Model    = mc$model,
  `num.lv` = mc$num_lv,
  Plants   = ifelse(mc$plants, "yes", "no"),
  logLik   = round(mc$logLik, 1),
  AIC      = round(mc$AIC, 1),
  dAIC     = round(mc$dAIC, 1),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S18. GLLVM H3 model comparison (AIC). Latent variables add nothing beyond the sample random effect (num.lv = 0 preferred among the plant models), and — notably — the null model with no plant predictors is itself AIC-preferred over the plant models (dAIC ≈ 117): the per-OTU plant slopes do not improve fit enough to justify their parameters, an independent echo of the 'too weak to resolve' result of Section 7.2.")
```

![](figures/gllvm_H3_perOTU_plant_coef.png)

**Figure S13**: Per-OTU fixed plant slopes (GLLVM, log scale; red = positive, blue = negative) for the 30 well-estimated OTUs, rows ordered by specificity and grouped by FUNGuild guild class — the frequentist counterpart of Figure S11. As in the Bayesian model, the coprophilous taxa covary *positively* with *Vaccinium* rather than diffusely.

```{r tab-h3g-spec}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
si <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_specificity_index.csv", check.names = FALSE)
si_disp <- si %>% filter(!separation) %>% head(12)
kable(data.frame(
  OTU            = si_disp$OTU_ID,
  Genus          = ifelse(is.na(si_disp$Genus), "—", si_disp$Genus),
  `Prev. (/30)`  = si_disp$prevalence,
  Specificity    = round(si_disp$specificity_HHI, 2),
  `Top plant`    = si_disp$dominant_plant,
  `Top slope [90% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", si_disp$dom_slope_med,
                                 si_disp$dom_slope_lwr90, si_disp$dom_slope_upr90),
  Resolved       = ifelse(si_disp$resolved_single_plant, "yes", "—"),
  Guild          = si_disp$guild_group,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S19. The twelve most plant-specific well-estimated OTUs under the GLLVM, ranked by Herfindahl specificity. Without the Bayesian model's shrinkage the unpooled Wald intervals resolve many more single-plant slopes; the strongest resolved coprophilous signal is Sporormiella (OTU636) with Vaccinium. Diffuse baseline (six genera) = 0.17.")
```

**Result.** The GLLVM reaches the **same verdict as the Bayesian model — H3 is not supported** — and does so through instructively different intermediate numbers. Because the fixed-slope estimator applies no shrinkage, its Wald intervals resolve **15 of the 30** well-estimated OTUs to a single-plant association (versus 1 of 46 under the pooled Bayesian model). But those resolved associations are spread across guilds rather than concentrated in the non-coprophilous taxa H3 predicts, so they do *not* produce the specificity difference the hypothesis requires. On the preregistered contrast the coprophilous group is **not** resolvably more diffuse than the plant-associated group: median specificity 0.21 (coprophilous) vs 0.24 (plant-associated), one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.42, and propagating the Wald uncertainty P(coprophilous more diffuse) = 0.64 — straddling the no-difference value of 0.5. The genus-list sensitivity grouping runs the other way (0.25 vs 0.24, p = 0.81). And, as above, AIC prefers the plant-free null model outright. The strongest resolved coprophilous signal is again a *positive Vaccinium* slope — here *Sporormiella* (OTU636, +12.3, 90 % CI \[6.7, 17.8\]), the *Sporormiella* counterpart of the Bayesian model's *Vaccinium*–*Thelebolus* signal — the opposite of the diffuse, passenger-free pattern H3 expects of a dung specialist.

![](figures/gllvm_H3_specificity_contrast.png)

**Figure S14**: Per-OTU GLLVM specificity by FUNGuild guild class (frequentist counterpart of Figure S12). Coprophilous OTUs are not resolvably more diffuse than plant-associated ones. Dashed line = maximally-diffuse baseline (1/6).

```{r tab-h3g-contrast}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
ct <- read.csv("tables/gllvm_H3_specificity_contrast.csv", check.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  Grouping                    = ct$grouping,
  `n copro`                   = ct$n_coprophilous,
  `n plant-assoc`             = ct$n_plant_assoc,
  `Copro HHI`                 = round(ct$copro_spec_med, 2),
  `Plant-assoc HHI`           = round(ct$plant_spec_med, 2),
  `Wilcoxon p (copro<plant)`  = round(ct$wilcox_p_copro_lower, 2),
  `P(copro more diffuse)`     = round(ct$P_copro_lower, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Table S20. GLLVM coprophilous-vs-plant-associated specificity contrast (FUNGuild primary; COPRO_GENERA genus list as sensitivity), the frequentist counterpart of Table S16. Neither grouping supports the predicted 'coprophilous more diffuse' direction. The full per-OTU × plant coefficient table (with Wald z, p and BH-q) is provided as tables/gllvm_H3_perOTU_plant_coef.csv.")
```

**Interpretation.** Two independent frameworks — a partial-pooling Bayesian joint model and an unpooled frequentist GLLVM — give the same answer: recognised coprophilous taxa are **not** more diffuse in their plant associations than other taxa, so H3 as preregistered is not supported, and the one robust piece of ecology (a positive coprophile–*Vaccinium* covariation, *Thelebolus* under one model, *Sporormiella* under the other) is the reverse of the ingested-passenger signature the test was built to detect. The two models disagree only on how many single-plant slopes count as "resolved," and that gap is exactly the expected footprint of shrinkage — the pooled model is conservative, the unpooled one liberal — not an ecological disagreement. Consistent with the forward-directional inference rule, neither the sparse Bayesian resolutions nor the plentiful GLLVM ones are read as evidence about gut residency; the honest reading remains that these winter-browse plants and the persistent dung-fungal core co-vary as parallel seasonal signatures, and that a larger, more diet-even matched sample is needed to test single-taxon passenger transport directly.
