## Section 8: Functional guilds — FUNGuild {.page-break-before}

Sections 3–6 characterise the seasonal shift *taxonomically* — which lineages turn over between winter and summer. This section asks what that community **does**: each OTU is assigned to a functional guild, and the guild composition of the dung mycobiome is compared across seasons. It is the descriptive counterpart to Section 9, which puts the same trait → season link inside a joint species distribution model. The two are deliberately built on the **same classification rule** so their results are directly comparable, but they differ in scope: Section 8 works on read shares across **all 1129 OTUs** of the canonical 52-sample object (no prevalence filter, because this is a description of where the reads go), whereas Section 9 models the 226 OTUs that pass its prevalence threshold. All results here are produced by `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R`.

### 8.1 Guild assignment and the classification rule

Guild annotation uses **FUNGuild** (Nguyen et al. 2016), run through its command-line tool against each OTU's own taxonomy string, so that assignments are made at the finest rank available per OTU (species, genus, family or order) rather than by a single-rank lookup. **693 of the 1129 canonical OTUs (61.4%) receive a guild call** at a usable confidence ranking; the remaining 436 return no assignment — either because no matching taxonomy record exists in the FUNGuild database or because the match carries no ranked guild.

FUNGuild returns compound guild strings rather than a single label — for example `|Dung Saprotroph|-Endophyte-Plant Saprotroph-Undefined Saprotroph`. OTUs are collapsed to a single class by a priority rule (first match wins): dung saprotroph → plant-associated → pathotroph, with anything else falling to *other assigned* or *unassigned* (no FUNGuild call at all). Coprophily takes precedence deliberately: it is the guild the study is about, and it would otherwise be absorbed into a generic saprotroph category. An OTU counts as a dung saprotroph if FUNGuild lists `Dung Saprotroph` **or** its genus is one of fourteen recognised coprophilous genera (the Section 3.2 list, omitting *Sporormia*, *Psathyrella* and *Stropharia*). That difference is immaterial here: *Sporormia* is absent from the dataset, both *Stropharia* OTUs are already assigned by their FUNGuild string, and the two *Psathyrella* OTUs carry 0.04% of reads, so no guild share below changes at the reported precision. This is the identical rule used for the Section 9 guild trait.

```{r tab-guild-crosswalk}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
cw <- read.csv("tables/guild_scheme_crosswalk.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lv <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
        "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
cw <- cw[order(match(cw$guild_display, lv)), ]
kable(data.frame(
  `Guild (Section 8)`      = cw$guild_display,
  `Class (Section 9)`     = cw$guild_class,
  `n OTUs`                 = cw$n_OTUs,
  Note                     = cw$note,
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-GUILDa. Crosswalk between the Section 8 display guilds and the Section 9 model trait, with OTU counts (1129 canonical OTUs). The two schemes are the same priority rule; they differ only in that Section 9's `other` class is split here according to whether the OTU carries a FUNGuild annotation at all.")
```

### 8.2 Guild composition shifts sharply between seasons

![](figures/Fig1_guild_season.png)

**Figure S-GUILDa**: Functional-guild composition of the dung mycobiome. **(A)** Per-sample guild read share, one stacked bar per dung sample, faceted by season and ordered within each season by dung-saprotroph share. **(B)** Per-sample read share by guild and season; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, and marks give the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum result (\* q \< 0.05, \*\* q \< 0.01, ns = not significant). **(C)** Mean guild read share by season and year, showing that the shift recurs in all three years. Colours are the Okabe–Ito colourblind-safe palette throughout.

Panels **(A)** and **(B)** here are the same object, rule and test as main-text **Fig. 1B–C** (Section 10.1) — the same result, not a second analysis. This figure is retained because panel **(C)**, the Season × Year consistency check of Section 8.3, has no main-text counterpart.

The seasonal contrast is large and concerns primarily two of the five guilds. **Dung saprotrophs rise from 13.6% of winter reads to 51.5% in summer**, while the **unassigned/dark fraction falls from 51.1% to 21.0%** — that is, roughly half of a typical winter sample consists of reads that FUNGuild cannot place at all, whereas a typical summer sample is dominated by recognised coprophilous fungi. Equivalently, the proportion of reads landing on a guild-annotated OTU rises from **49% in winter to 79% in summer**.

```{r tab-guild-season}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
g <- read.csv("tables/guild_season_readshare.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
kable(data.frame(
  Guild            = g$Guild,
  `Summer mean %`  = pc(g$mean_summer),
  `Winter mean %`  = pc(g$mean_winter),
  `Summer median %`= pc(g$median_summer),
  `Winter median %`= pc(g$median_winter),
  `Detected (S/W)` = paste0(g$prevalence_summer, "/", g$prevalence_winter),
  `p`              = signif(g$p_value, 2),
  `q (BH)`         = ifelse(is.na(g$q_value), "—", signif(g$q_value, 2)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-GUILDb. Per-sample guild read shares by season (26 samples per season), with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment across the five guilds. 'Detected' gives the number of samples in which the guild occurs at all. The final row is a robustness check, not part of the BH family: it restricts the dung-saprotroph guild to OTUs matching a recognised coprophilous genus, discarding those assigned on the FUNGuild string alone.")
```

**The dung-saprotroph result does not depend on how generously that guild is defined.** The rule counts an OTU as coprophilous if FUNGuild lists `Dung Saprotroph` *or* its genus is a recognised coprophilous genus. Restricting it to the genus criterion alone drops 24 of the 37 OTUs (37 across all 1129 canonical OTUs; the 14 dung saprotrophs of the Section 9 model are those of the 37 that pass its ≥ 5-replicate prevalence filter) and still gives **45.7% summer versus 8.5% winter** (p = 0.00094; final row of Table S-GUILDb). The signal is concentrated in a few abundant taxa — OTU1 (*Thelebolus*), OTU636 (*Sporormiella*) and OTU1225 (*Coniochaeta*) are the three largest contributors — which is consistent with the dominance analysis of Section 5.4 and with the differential-abundance results of Section 6, where *Sporormiella* OTU636 and *Coniochaeta* OTU1225 are both significantly summer-elevated.

### 8.3 The guild shift recurs in all three years

```{r tab-guild-year}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
sy <- read.csv("tables/guild_season_year_readshare.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lv <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
        "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
cells <- c("Winter 2022","Winter 2023","Winter 2024","Summer 2022","Summer 2023","Summer 2024")
sy$cell <- factor(paste(sy$Season, sy$Year), levels = cells)
mat <- tapply(sy$mean_share, list(factor(sy$Guild, levels = lv), sy$cell),
              function(z) z[1])
kable(cbind(Guild = lv, as.data.frame(round(100 * mat, 1), check.names = FALSE)),
      row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-GUILDc. Mean per-sample guild read share (%) by season and year. Cell sizes: winter 10/9/7 and summer 9/9/8 samples for 2022/2023/2024.")
```

Panel C of Figure S-GUILDa and Table S-GUILDc show the same ordering in every year: **the dung-saprotroph share is higher in summer than in winter in 2022, 2023 and 2024** (41.3% vs 24.5%, 68.3% vs 10.9%, and 44.0% vs 1.7% respectively). Within-year tests are significant for 2023 (q = 0.027) and marginal for 2024 (q = 0.053) but not for 2022 (q = 0.74), where two unusually coprophile-rich winter samples raise the winter mean and its variance. The direction is therefore consistent across all three years while the magnitude varies. This is the functional-guild analogue of the H1 result in Section 4.2, and the two agree closely: the compositional Season × Year interaction is significant there (p = 0.011; four of five distance measures, marginal under the fifth, Table S7b), and the per-year breakdown ranks the years in the same order as the guild data — 2023 strongest, 2024 intermediate, 2022 weakest (Table S5b). Given three years and modest per-cell sample sizes, the safe reading is that the seasonal shift is directionally reproducible but of year-varying magnitude, not that it has a constant effect size.

::: {.callout-note when-profile="docs"}
**Interpretation and caveats.**

**What this adds.** The guild layer reproduces the seasonal signal independently of taxonomy and gives it a functional reading: summer dung supports an actively coprophilous community, winter dung does not. Section 9 tests the same link within a joint model and reaches a concordant conclusion — guild predicts seasonal *occurrence*, with dung saprotrophs more likely to occur in summer (posterior support 0.96) — so the descriptive and model-based views agree.

**Relation to the dark taxa (E1).** The winter unassigned share here (51.1%) closely tracks the dark-taxa share reported in Section 3.4 (51.3% of winter reads), but the two are **not the same set**: "unassigned" here means no FUNGuild annotation (436 OTUs), while "dark" in Section 3.4 means no confident genus in the canonical taxonomy (493 OTUs). They share 390 OTUs, and 103 OTUs lack a genus yet still receive a FUNGuild call at family or order level. The definitions coincide in winter but diverge in summer (21.0% unassigned versus 31.2% dark), so the two figures should not be used interchangeably. Section 3.4 establishes that a substantial part of this winter fraction is genuinely novel rather than merely absent from reference databases; the functional consequence is that **winter guild composition is the least well characterised part of this dataset**, and its apparent depletion of coprophiles is partly a statement about annotation coverage.

**Limitations.** (i) Read share is not biomass: PCR and copy-number biases mean these proportions describe sequence abundance, not fungal abundance. (ii) FUNGuild assignments are database-derived and inherit its taxonomic and geographic biases; assignments made at family or order level are necessarily coarser than species-level ones, and confidence rankings (Table S-GUILDb does not stratify by them) are `Probable` for the majority of assigned OTUs. (iii) The compositional constraint discussed above means that a guild's decline in relative terms need not imply any absolute decline. (iv) A guild label describes an ecological capability inferred from relatives, not a verified activity in this substrate.

**Supersedes.** The preliminary guild percentages previously recorded in this section were an interim workspace check that predated the finalized script; they were not reproducible from any committed code. The values above are produced by `Scripts/8_functional_guilds.R` and are reproducible from the staged CSVs in `tables/`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Section 9's residual `other` class mixes OTUs that *do* carry a FUNGuild call with 46 that have a taxonomic genus but **no** guild annotation at all; the latter carry roughly a tenth of winter reads. That conflation is harmless for a model trait but misleading in a read-share figure, so the two are separated here into **Other assigned** and folded into **Unassigned / dark** respectively. Table S-GUILDa reconciles the two schemes.

**Why FUNGuild and not FungalTraits.** Both annotation sources were built and compared. `fungaltraits_otu` (genus-level lookup via the `fungaltraits` package) covers 195 of 1129 OTUs (17%) and is a **strict subset** of the FUNGuild annotation (693 of the 1129 canonical OTUs, 61%) — it contributes no unique coverage. On the 195 OTUs both annotate they agree on the exact `Guild` string only 37% of the time (49% on trophic mode), because collapsing to one record per genus discards the species-level resolution FUNGuild's per-OTU run retains. FUNGuild is therefore used as the sole guild source; FungalTraits is retained only as a coarse sensitivity check, and guild calls are never merged between the two for the same OTU.

**Means and medians tell different parts of this story, and both are reported.** For the plant-associated and pathotroph guilds the seasonal *means* are nearly identical (18.0% vs 23.4%, and 4.7% vs 5.8%) while the *medians* differ several-fold (2.1% vs 18.4%, and 0.1% vs 3.8%). The rank-based tests follow the medians and are significant for both. The reason is compositional rather than ecological: because dung saprotrophs occupy so much of a typical summer sample, every other guild is compressed toward zero in most summer samples, while a small number of summer samples in which coprophiles are absent carry large plant-associated or pathotroph fractions and pull the summer means back up. These guilds are better described as **relatively displaced in summer** than as absolute winter specialists — a limitation inherent to read shares, which are constrained to sum to one.
:::

## Section 9: Joint species distribution model — HMSC (H1 synthesis) {.page-break-before}

Sections 4–6 treat the seasonal signal one lens at a time: community dissimilarity (H1), per-sample diversity (H2), and per-OTU differential abundance (GLLVM). This section brings them into a single hierarchical model. We fit a joint species distribution model (HMSC — Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities; `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`) that simultaneously (i) partitions each OTU's variance among Season, Year, and the nested sampling structure; (ii) asks whether an OTU's functional guild predicts how it responds to Season (the trait → environment link); (iii) recovers each OTU's seasonal niche for a like-for-like cross-check against the Section-6 GLLVM; (iv) estimates the residual co-occurrence left once Season, Year and traits are accounted for; and (v) tests for phylogenetic signal in seasonal niches. It is the model-based synthesis of the H1 story, fitted directly on the corrected canonical data (unlike the Section-6 GLLVM, which predates the depth-filter fix).

### 9.1 Model, design, and what is (and isn't) trustworthy

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29 (model revision): rewrite freely -->
The models use the one-row-per-PCR-replicate object (`alldat_full$nopool`; 109 replicate rows from 55 biological dung samples), retaining the **226 OTUs present in ≥ 5 replicates** — the same prevalence rule used for the GLLVM/H3 analyses. Fixed effects are **Season** (winter as reference) **+ Year**; the species trait is the five-level functional **guild** class derived from FUNGuild (dung saprotroph, plant-associated, pathotroph, dark/unassigned, other — assigned by the priority rule in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`, counts below). Three models are fitted:

- **Headline — CLR abundance, replicates averaged.** Each PCR replicate is CLR-transformed (the compositional normalisation that stands in for a library-size offset), and the two replicates of a dropping are then averaged, giving one row per dropping (55 rows). The random level is the **biological sample** (the dropping), with two latent factors. This model carries the abundance results of this section and both panels of Figure 3.
- **Complement — CLR abundance, replicate level.** The same CLR response with both replicates kept as rows (109 rows), and **two random levels**: biological sample (two latent factors) and **PCR replicate** (one latent factor).
- **Robustness — presence/absence (probit)**, replicate level, with biological sample and PCR replicate as random levels.

Both CLR models scale each OTU's response to unit variance before fitting and cap the number of latent factors; the reason for the cap, and for the choice of headline, is given below Table S-HMSCb.

```{r tab-hmsc-guild}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
og <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_otu_guild.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gt <- as.data.frame(table(factor(og$guild_class,
        levels = c("dung_saprotroph","plant_associated","pathotroph","dark_unassigned","other"))))
kable(data.frame(`Guild group` = gt$Var1, `n OTUs` = gt$Freq, check.names = FALSE),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCa. Functional-guild composition of the 226 modelled OTUs. FUNGuild returns a compound guild string per OTU; these are resolved to one class by the hierarchical priority rule in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`, shared verbatim with Section 8. Dark/unassigned and 'other' together dominate the count — the modest coprophilous set (14 OTUs) nonetheless carries the strongest seasonal signal (Sections 9.3–9.4).")
```

An **individual-bird** random level was deliberately **not** included. Microsatellite genotyping succeeded for only a handful of repeat birds, so a bird level (with unidentified droppings entered as singletons) would have \~51 units against 55 biological samples — effectively one-to-one with the sample level, confounding the two sets of latent factors. In the three-level version this stopped the CLR community-level parameters from converging and made the variance partition unstable, so the bird level was dropped, leaving sample + PCR (mirroring the GLLVM's `(1 | Sample_ID_field)`). Dropping it was not by itself sufficient; see the note below Table S-HMSCb. Each model was fitted with four chains (1000 samples, thinning 50, 25,000 transient iterations).

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29 (why the headline model wins): rewrite freely -->
::: callout-note
**Why the replicate-averaged model is the headline.** An earlier version of this section used a single CLR model at the replicate level with an uncapped number of latent factors (seven at the sample level, five at the PCR level). Its four chains converged to four different answers (Table S-HMSCb2): the *Thelebolus* Season coefficient was 0.36, 3.03, 0.69 and −0.03 in the four chains, and the Season share of variance between 5% and 28%. The PSRF understated the problem because each chain mixed well within its own solution. The cause is structural. Season is constant within a dropping, so enough sample-level latent factors can reproduce the Season contrast themselves, and each chain divided the seasonal signal differently between the Season coefficients and the latent factors. Longer chains do not cure this; capping the number of latent factors does, and both CLR models reported here are capped.

With the cap, both CLR models converge on the Season effects (Table S-HMSCb). They differ in how they treat the two PCR replicates of each dropping. The replicate-level model estimates PCR replicate as its own random level, but the split of variance between dropping and replicate rests on only 54 replicate pairs and is weakly identified: in an earlier independent fit with the identical specification, its chains settled in two different splits (dropping/PCR 0.52/0.14 in two chains, 0.43/0.27 in the other two), whereas in the fit reported here the chains agree (Table S-HMSCc3). The replicate-level model also counts the two replicates as partly independent observations, which narrows its credible intervals (median width 0.84 of the headline model's; Table S-HMSCc4). Averaging the replicates removes both issues by construction — one row per dropping, no replicate-level split to identify — and its chains agree to within 0.003 on every reported guild mean and variance component.

The two models agree on what the figures report: per-OTU Season coefficients correlate at Pearson r = 0.97 (Spearman ρ = 0.89), and 56 OTUs have a 95% credible interval excluding zero in both (Table S-HMSCc4). The replicate-level model is therefore kept as the complement that carries an explicit PCR-replicate level, and the PCR-replicate variance the headline model averages away is measured directly in Section 9.2 (Table S-HMSCc2).

The **probit (occurrence)** model was not refitted. Its PSRFs are low (Beta median 1.01, 99.6% below 1.1), but compared chain by chain its guild means differ by up to 0.24 on the probit scale — the same qualitative answer in every chain, with looser agreement than the CLR models.
:::

### 9.2 Variance partitioning: a reproducible seasonal axis within large individual heterogeneity

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29 (numbers updated to the revised model): rewrite freely -->
For every OTU the headline model decomposes the variance it explains in CLR abundance into contributions from Season, Year, and the biological-sample (dropping) random level. Averaged across OTUs, **Season accounts for 31.5% and Year for 18.5%**, with the remaining 49.9% carried by differences among droppings. These are shares of the variance the model explains, not of total variance, so they are not comparable with a PERMANOVA R².

![](figures/hmsc_variance_partition.png)

**Figure S-HMSCa**: Per-OTU variance partitioning (CLR abundance, headline model). Each vertical bar is one OTU; colours give the proportion of that OTU's explained variance attributable to Season, Year and the biological-sample random level. Individual-dropping heterogeneity is the single largest component.

```{r tab-hmsc-vp}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
vp <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_variance_partition.csv", check.names = FALSE)
comp <- c("Season","Year","Random: sample")
cw  <- colMeans(vp[, comp])
byg <- aggregate(vp[, comp], list(Guild = vp$guild), mean)
tabb <- rbind(data.frame(Guild = "all OTUs (community mean)", t(cw), check.names = FALSE), byg)
tabb[, comp] <- round(tabb[, comp] * 100, 1)
pcr <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tabb$pcr <- round(100 * pcr$share_total_mean[match(sub("all OTUs \\(community mean\\)", "all", tabb$Guild), pcr$group)], 1)
kable(tabb, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Guild group", "Season %", "Year %", "Dropping %", "PCR replicate % (model-free)"),
      caption = "Table S-HMSCc. Mean percentage of per-OTU variance attributed to each component of the headline model, community-wide and by guild; the three model components sum to 100%. The last column is not part of that partition: it is the model-free share of each OTU's total CLR variance that lies between the two PCR replicates of a dropping (Table S-HMSCc2).")
```

For each OTU, replicate variance = mean(d²)/2, where d is the CLR difference between the two replicates; the share divides it by the OTU's total CLR variance and is averaged over OTUs (95% CI: 500 bootstrap resamples of droppings). 'Detected in only one replicate' is the fraction of droppings containing the OTU in which only one replicate detected it; the last column repeats the share using only droppings where both did. Per-OTU values: tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance_perOTU.csv.")

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29: rewrite freely -->
The ecological reading is two-sided but coherent. The **seasonal axis is real and reproducible**, yet at the level of an individual OTU the largest single component is still *how much dung communities differ from one dropping to the next*. HMSC formalises what the ordination and dominance analyses already suggested: season shifts the community in a consistent direction, on top of large individual-level variability. This decomposition, broken down by guild exactly as in Table S-HMSCc, is Figure 3B of the main text (Section 10.3).

**PCR-replicate variance.** Because the headline model averages the two PCR replicates of each dropping, it has no PCR level to partition. The replicate-to-replicate variance is measured instead, outside the model, from the 54 droppings with two replicates (Table S-HMSCc2). Both replicates come from the same DNA extract, so any difference between them is measurement noise. For each OTU, half the mean squared difference between the two replicates' CLR values estimates the replicate variance; divided by the OTU's total CLR variance and averaged over OTUs, **replicate noise accounts for 32% of CLR variance** (bootstrap 95% CI 28–40%; median over OTUs 25%). The estimate does not depend on the method: dividing instead by the variance left after Season and Year gives 36%, and a per-OTU mixed model with a dropping random intercept gives 34% (per-OTU correlation with the former 0.998). Nor is it driven by unequal sequencing depth: the two replicates differ in depth by a median factor of 1.31, and the size of that difference does not predict how different the replicates look (Spearman ρ = 0.21, p = 0.13, n = 54). It is not spread evenly, however. Coprophilous dung saprotrophs are the most repeatable guild (17%, CI 11–25%) and pathotrophs the least (50%, CI 36–62%).

The replicate noise is almost entirely **detection**, not abundance. Where both replicates detect an OTU, their CLR values agree closely: replicate noise is then a median 3% of variance. But in 46% of the droppings in which an OTU is found, only one of the two replicates detects it — the signature of low-abundance taxa near the detection limit, where PCR and sequencing sampling decide whether a few reads appear. Coprophiles are detected in both replicates more consistently (only one replicate detects them in 32% of cases) and, when both detect them, differ by a median 1% of variance: where *Thelebolus* or *Sporormiella* is present, both replicates see it at similar levels. The complementary replicate-level model, which fits PCR replicate as a random level, gives a comparable picture: 27% of its explained variance at the PCR level, 43% at the dropping level, and a Season share of 17.5% (Table S-HMSCc3). Its Season share is lower than the headline model's because replicate noise, which the headline model averages away, enters its denominator.

### 9.3 Guild predicts seasonal occurrence — the coprophilous summer signature, formalised

The trait → environment matrix (Gamma) asks whether an OTU's guild predicts its seasonal response. Read from the well-converged probit model, it does. Relative to the winter reference, **dung saprotrophs are markedly more likely to occur in summer** (the reference-guild Season effect is positive with posterior support 0.96), and the yeast-rich "other" group shows the same direction (support 0.83); **pathotrophs lean the opposite way**, toward winter (support 0.85 in the negative direction). Plant-associated and dark/unassigned taxa show no clear guild-level seasonal preference.

![](figures/hmsc_probit_gamma.png)

**Figure S-HMSCb**: Trait → environment link (Gamma) from the probit occurrence model. Cells show the posterior support for each guild's response to Season and Year; the dung-saprotroph summer signal and the guild-structured Year (2024) shift are the supported effects. Red = positive (summer / higher), blue = negative.

```{r tab-hmsc-gamma}

g <- g[g$covariate == "Seasonsummer", ]
g$trait <- sub("^guild", "", g$trait)
g$trait[g$trait == "(Intercept)"] <- "dung saprotroph (reference)"

  `Guild (trait)` = g$trait,
  `Gamma (summer)` = round(g$mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", g$CrI_2.5, g$CrI_97.5),
  `Support P(>0)` = round(g$support, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCd. Probit Gamma — guild trait → probability of summer occurrence. The reference row is the dung-saprotroph guild's own Season effect; the other rows are deviations from it. Support is the posterior probability that the coefficient exceeds zero (values near 1 = summer, near 0 = winter).")
```

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29: rewrite freely -->
On the abundance scale the same link can now be read from the headline model, whose Gamma converges (Table S-HMSCb), and it is sharper (Table S-HMSCd2). The dung-saprotroph guild's own Season effect is positive (+0.31 in standardised units, 95% CrI \[0.07, 0.54\], support 0.994). Plant-associated, pathotroph and dark/unassigned OTUs all respond clearly less summer-ward than dung saprotrophs (differences −0.37, −0.52 and −0.46; support ≤ 0.004), while the "other" group does not differ clearly from them (−0.16, support 0.12).

This is the guild-level counterpart to the taxonomic and dominance results (Sections 3.2, 5.4): the recognised coprophilous fungi — *Sporormiella*, *Thelebolus*, *Coniochaeta* — are not a fixed cold-adapted core but a **summer-occurring dung guild**, consistent with the richer, more fungal-propagule-laden summer diet. HMSC states that pattern as a trait effect estimated across all 226 OTUs at once, rather than genus by genus.

### 9.4 Per-OTU seasonal niches, and agreement with the GLLVM

Extracting each OTU's Season coefficient (Beta) from the headline CLR model recovers the same lineages at the individual level. The **three most strongly summer-shifted OTUs are the coprophilous dung saprotrophs** *Thelebolus* (OTU1), *Sporormiella* (OTU636) and *Coniochaeta* (OTU1225), each with a 95% credible interval well clear of zero — while the **most strongly winter-shifted OTUs are dark/unassigned taxa**, led by OTU1369, the same taxonomically unresolved Dothideomycete that anchors winter dominance in Sections 5.4 and the E1 dark-taxa analysis (Section 3.4).

![](figures/hmsc_beta_season.png)

**Figure S-HMSCc**: Per-OTU seasonal niche (HMSC CLR Beta on Season; positive = summer), for the 25 most summer- and 25 most winter-shifted OTUs, coloured by guild, with 95% credible intervals. The summer extreme is dominated by dung saprotrophs (warm) and yeasts; the winter extreme by dark/unassigned taxa. This is the same model and the same quantity as Figure 3A of the main text (Section 10.3), but selected differently and deliberately kept alongside it: here all 226 OTUs are ranked by effect size, so the panel shows the community's extremes regardless of how rare they are, whereas Figure 3A restricts to the 22 OTUs holding at least 1% of modelled read share each and adds a guild-mean block. Rare OTUs with large coefficients therefore appear here and not there.

```{r tab-hmsc-beta}
#| echo: false
suppressMessages(library(dplyr)); library(knitr)
b <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fmt <- function(d) d %>% transmute(
  OTU = OTU_ID, Genus = ifelse(is.na(Genus), "—", Genus), Guild = guild,
  Beta = round(beta_season_mean, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", beta_season_CrI2.5, beta_season_CrI97.5),
  Support = round(beta_season_support, 2))
kable(b %>% arrange(desc(beta_season_mean)) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmt(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(i). Most strongly summer-shifted OTUs (HMSC CLR Beta on Season).")
kable(b %>% arrange(beta_season_mean) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% fmt(), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table S-HMSCe(ii). Most strongly winter-shifted OTUs. Beta is in CLR units (the model's standardised coefficient multiplied by the OTU's CLR standard deviation). Full table: tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv.")
```

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29 (numbers updated to the revised model): rewrite freely -->
The same per-OTU niche can be estimated on the **occurrence** scale, with the probit model. There, 55 of the 226 OTUs have a Season coefficient whose 95% credible interval excludes zero, against 74 in the headline abundance model. The two formulations rank the community's seasonal responses consistently (Spearman ρ = 0.76), and the probit per-OTU estimates aggregate to the guild-level Gamma of Section 9.3 to within 0.04, so nothing here contradicts the results above. What the occurrence scale does change is *which* taxa sit at the summer extreme. In abundance the coprophiles lead outright; in occurrence the shift is community-wide (157 of 226 OTUs point towards summer, median +0.70) and the extreme is occupied by cold-adapted basidiomycete yeasts — *Vishniacozyma*, *Mrakia*, *Piskurozyma*, *Phenoliferia* — with *Sporormiella* (OTU636) the only dung saprotroph in the top 25 and the mean dung-saprotroph rank falling to 125 of 226 (from 59 in abundance). The distinction is ecologically substantive rather than a modelling artefact: coprophilous fungi are what summer dung is largely *made of* in read share, but they are not the taxa that most reliably *appear* in summer. The winter extreme is unchanged and, if anything, more strongly resolved — dark/unassigned taxa and pathotrophs, with OTU1369 the most winter-shifted OTU in the community (β = −2.25, 95% CrI \[−3.53, −1.08\]). Both scales are carried forward, but they are not given equal weight in the main text. Figure 3 in Section 10.3 is built entirely on the abundance formulation — the scale on which the coprophilous shift is the community's largest seasonal effect, and the scale that Figures 1 and 2 also work on — while the occurrence-scale result reported here stays supplementary, alongside Tables S-HMSCe(iii) and S-HMSCe(iv). The abundance-scale table above also remains the one comparable with the GLLVM below.

Because the GLLVM (Section 6) is an independent model — negative-binomial counts rather than CLR abundance, a different random-effect structure, and fitted on a different OTU snapshot — the two provide a genuine cross-method check. Their per-OTU Season coefficients agree well.

![](figures/hmsc_vs_gllvm_season.png)

**Figure S-HMSCd**: HMSC (CLR Beta) versus GLLVM Season coefficient, one point per shared OTU (n = 139 after excluding the GLLVM's on/off near-separation OTUs, whose ±10³ coefficients are not comparable), coloured by guild. The two independent joint models rank the OTUs' seasonal responses consistently (**Spearman ρ = 0.75**), a strong convergent-validity result for H1 at OTU resolution.

### 9.5 Residual co-occurrence beyond Season

The biological-sample latent factors capture the co-occurrence structure that remains once Season, Year and guild are accounted for — pairs of OTUs that rise and fall together across droppings for reasons the fixed effects do not explain.

![](figures/hmsc_omega_sample.png)

**Figure S-HMSCe**: Residual OTU–OTU association matrix (biological-sample level), showing only associations supported at ≥ 0.95 posterior probability and restricted to OTUs with at least one such association, ordered by hierarchical clustering. Red = positive residual co-occurrence, blue = negative. Blocks of positively associated OTUs indicate sub-communities that track together beyond the seasonal signal — candidate co-dispersed or co-sourced groups for follow-up.

### 9.6 Phylogenetic signal in seasonal niches

::: callout-warning
**Not yet re-run on the revised model (2026-09-29).** The phylogenetic variant below was fitted on the superseded, non-converged CLR structure (Section 9.1). Its ρ and the correlations with the main model in Table S-HMSCf refer to that structure. Re-fitting it on the headline model is pending a decision (`HMSC_RUN_PHYLO=1` in `Scripts/10_hmsc.R`).
:::

Adding the OTU phylogeny to the CLR model estimates rho, the degree to which closely related fungi share environmental niches. The signal is substantial and well-identified.

```{r tab-hmsc-rho}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
rh <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_rho_phylo.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(
  `ρ (median)` = round(rh$median, 2),
  `95% CrI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", rh$CrI_2.5, rh$CrI_97.5),
  `P(ρ>0)` = rh$P_gt0, ESS = rh$ess, PSRF = round(rh$psrf, 2),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCf. Phylogenetic signal parameter ρ from the phylogeny-augmented CLR model. Adding the phylogeny leaves the per-OTU niches and trait link essentially unchanged (Beta / Gamma correlation with the main model ≈ 0.94 / 0.90), so ρ is a genuine additional signal rather than a re-description of the fixed effects.")
```

With **ρ ≈ 0.72 (95% CrI \[0.60, 0.80\], P(ρ \> 0) = 1)**, seasonal niches are **phylogenetically conserved**: related lineages tend to shift together between winter and summer. This dovetails with the guild result — because guild is itself partly phylogenetically structured, the coprophilous summer signature is echoed as a broader phylogenetic pattern. It is reported as a secondary, exploratory result (the phylogeny-augmented model is a supplementary variant), but it is a clean, non-trivial one.

### 9.7 What the model predicts — and its honest limit

Finally, HMSC quantifies how much of the community it actually explains, in-sample versus out-of-sample (two-fold cross-validation, with folds split by biological sample so PCR replicates never leak across folds).

![](figures/hmsc_R2_explanatory_vs_cv.png)

**Figure S-HMSCf**: Explanatory (in-sample) versus two-fold cross-validated per-OTU R² for the CLR model. Points lie far below the 1:1 line: the model fits the observed communities well but does not predict held-out droppings.

```{r tab-hmsc-r2}
#| echo: false
library(knitr)
r2 <- read.csv("tables/hmsc_predictive_R2_summary.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lab <- c(clr = "CLR (abundance)", pa = "Probit (occurrence)")
kable(data.frame(
  Model = lab[r2$model],
  `Explanatory R²` = round(r2$mean_expl_R2, 3),
  `2-fold CV R²` = ifelse(is.na(r2$mean_cv_R2), "—", round(r2$mean_cv_R2, 3)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Table S-HMSCg. Community-mean explanatory vs cross-validated fit. Explanatory R² is moderate; cross-validated R² is near zero.")
```

The explanatory fit is moderate (community-mean R² ≈ 0.29 for the headline abundance model) but **cross-validated R² is near zero** (≈ 0.03) — the model does not predict the fungal community of a dropping it has not seen. Far from undercutting the story, this is the quantitative statement of it: the seasonal and guild effects documented above are **real and directional but small against the dominant, idiosyncratic variation among individual droppings**. A ptarmigan's dung mycobiome is shaped by season in a reproducible way, yet remains largely individual — which is exactly what a transient, diet- and propagule-sourced community should look like, and a useful caution for anyone hoping to read season directly off a single sample.

**In summary**, HMSC does not overturn any earlier result; it unifies them and adds two things the single-lens analyses could not: a variance decomposition that sizes the seasonal signal against individual heterogeneity, and a formal trait- and phylogeny-level account of *why* the seasonal turnover looks the way it does — a summer-occurring coprophilous dung guild, phylogenetically conserved, riding on top of large among-individual variability.

## Section 10: Main-text figures {.page-break-before}

::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
Sections 2–9 document the analyses in full. This section collects the figures that appear in the **main manuscript**, which present a deliberately reduced selection of those results for a general readership. It exists so that every main-text figure has exactly one authoritative definition.

**How this section works.**

-   Each main figure appears **once**, embedded from `figures/main/`, with its **full build code in the collapsible drop-down** beneath it (HTML version).
-   Every figure is written in three formats to the same stem: **`.png` and `.jpg` at 600 dpi** (raster, for whichever a submission system demands) and **`.pdf`** (vector, for print). The appendix embeds the PNG.
-   That code chunk **is the source of truth** for the figure. There is no parallel copy in `Scripts/`; nothing else generates these files.
-   The chunks are `eval: false`, so rendering this appendix never rebuilds a figure. To rebuild one after editing its chunk, run the runner from the `Supplementary/` directory:

``` bash
conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig1-build
```

-   Each figure carries a one-line **provenance cross-reference** naming the thematic sections its inputs come from.
-   The thematic sections keep their own supplementary version of a plot only where it is genuinely different (a different object, more ranks, unfiltered); where it would be the same object, they cross-reference here instead.

**File-naming rule.** Supplementary figure files begin with `S`; main-text figure files are `Fig<N>_<slug>` and live in `figures/main/`. (One legacy exception is pending: `figures/Fig1_guild_season.png` is the *supplementary* Figure S-GUILDa of Section 8 and is scheduled for renaming.)
:::

### 10.1 Figure 1 — Composition and function of the dung mycobiome

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
*Provenance: Fig. 1A uses the genus-level composition of Section 3.1; Fig. 1B–C the guild assignments of Section 8.2. All three panels are computed on the canonical 52-sample object (`alldat$nopool`), and A and B share one sample axis.*
::::

![](figures/main/Fig1_composition_function.png)

**Figure 1**: Composition and function of the willow ptarmigan dung mycobiome across seasons. **(A)** Per-sample genus-level read share — the nine most abundant genera, all remaining named genera pooled as *Other genera*, and reads on OTUs with no confident genus assignment as *Unassigned*. **(B)** Per-sample functional-guild read share for the **same 52 samples in the same order**, so each column is the same dropping in both panels; samples are ordered within each season by descending dung-saprotroph share. **(C)** Per-sample guild read share by season; boxes show the median and interquartile range, points are individual samples, and marks give the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum result across the five guilds (\* q \< 0.05, \*\* q \< 0.01, ns = not significant). *Thelebolus* in (A) and the dung-saprotroph guild in (B) intentionally share one colour — *Thelebolus* is that guild's dominant member — as do the two grey "no assignment" bands.

Read down a column and the two descriptions line up: the summer samples that are almost entirely dung saprotrophs in (B) are the samples dominated end-to-end by *Thelebolus*, *Sporormiella* and *Coniochaeta* in (A), while winter samples are a patchwork of many low-abundance genera sitting under a large unassigned fraction. The seasonal contrast is therefore the same result seen taxonomically and functionally: dung saprotrophs rise from 13.6% of winter reads to 51.5% in summer, and the unassigned fraction falls from 51.1% to 21.0% (panel C; Section 8.2). Panel A also makes the interpretive limit visible — roughly half of a typical winter sample is reads that carry no genus at all, which is the subject of the dark-taxa analysis in Section 3.4.

```{r fig1-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full build code for Figure 1 — the source of truth for figures/main/Fig1_composition_function.{png,pdf}"

# Figure 1 -- Composition and function of the dung mycobiome.
# Canonical object alldat$nopool (52 samples). Panels A and B share one sample
# axis; panel C tests the guild shares behind panel B.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig1-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(phyloseq); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})

rdata <- if (file.exists("eco_analysis.RData")) "eco_analysis.RData" else
         "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates/eco_analysis.RData"
load(rdata)
stopifnot(exists("alldat"), exists("funguild_otu"))   # funguild_otu <- 8_functional_guilds.R

out_dir <- "figures/main"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                  # headless: no X11 fallback

# ---- data ------------------------------------------------------------------
ps  <- alldat$nopool                                  # 52 samples, PCR reps summed
m   <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) m <- t(m)   # samples x taxa
rel <- m / rowSums(m)
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(rel) - 1) < 1e-10))

md     <- data.frame(as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
Season <- factor(c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer")[md$Season],
                 levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))
stopifnot(!anyNA(Season), identical(rownames(rel), rownames(m)))

strip_rank <- function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x)      # "g__Sporormiella" -> "Sporormiella"
tax <- data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gen <- strip_rank(tax$Genus[match(colnames(m), rownames(tax))])
gen <- ifelse(gen %in% c("", "NA"), NA, gen)

# ---- panel A categories: top genera + Other + Unassigned -------------------
N_GENERA  <- 9                                        # see the palette note below
by_genus  <- t(rowsum(t(rel), group = ifelse(is.na(gen), ".unassigned", gen)))
named     <- setdiff(colnames(by_genus), ".unassigned")
top       <- names(sort(colMeans(by_genus[, named, drop = FALSE]),
                        decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(N_GENERA)]
tidy_gen  <- function(x) sub("_gen_Incertae_sedis", " (unclass.)", x)

GEN_LEVELS <- c(tidy_gen(top), "Other genera", "Unassigned (no genus)")
gen_cat    <- ifelse(is.na(gen), "Unassigned (no genus)",
              ifelse(gen %in% top, tidy_gen(gen), "Other genera"))
gen_share  <- t(rowsum(t(rel), group = gen_cat))[, GEN_LEVELS, drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(gen_share) - 1) < 1e-10))

# ---- panel B categories: FUNGuild guilds -----------------------------------
# Rule verbatim from 8_functional_guilds.R (itself from 10_hmsc.R), so Figure 1,
# appendix Section 8 and Section 9 classify OTUs identically.
COPRO_GENERA <- c("Sordaria","Podospora","Cercophora","Chaetomium","Schizothecium",
                  "Preussia","Delitschia","Pilobolus","Ascobolus","Saccobolus",
                  "Sporormiella","Coprinopsis","Thelebolus","Coniochaeta")
guild_str <- funguild_otu$Guild[match(colnames(m), funguild_otu$OTU_ID)]
is_copro  <- (!is.na(guild_str) & grepl("Dung Saprotroph", guild_str)) |
             (!is.na(gen)       & gen %in% COPRO_GENERA)
is_plant  <- !is_copro & !is.na(guild_str) &
             grepl("Endophyte|Plant Saprotroph|Plant Pathogen|Epiphyte", guild_str)
is_patho  <- !is_copro & !is_plant & !is.na(guild_str) & grepl("Pathogen|Parasite", guild_str)

GUILD_LEVELS <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
                  "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
guild_cat <- ifelse(is_copro, "Dung saprotroph",
             ifelse(is_plant, "Plant-associated",
             ifelse(is_patho, "Pathotroph",
             ifelse(!is.na(guild_str), "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark"))))
guild_share <- t(rowsum(t(rel), group = guild_cat))[, GUILD_LEVELS, drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(guild_share) - 1) < 1e-10))

# ---- shared sample order: descending dung-saprotroph share within season ----
ord <- rownames(rel)[order(Season, -guild_share[, "Dung saprotroph"])]

to_long <- function(mat, levels) data.frame(
  SampleID = factor(rep(rownames(mat), times = ncol(mat)), levels = ord),
  Season   = rep(Season, times = ncol(mat)),
  Category = factor(rep(colnames(mat), each = nrow(mat)), levels = levels),
  share    = as.vector(mat), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
genL <- to_long(gen_share, GEN_LEVELS); guiL <- to_long(guild_share, GUILD_LEVELS)
stopifnot(identical(levels(genL$SampleID), levels(guiL$SampleID)))

# ---- palettes --------------------------------------------------------------
# Guilds and Season keep the repo's Okabe-Ito assignments (8_functional_guilds.R).
# The genus scale is a separate colourblind-checked set, validated on ALL pairs
# (worst CVD dE 7.4, worst normal-vision dE 15.6) -- which is why nine genera and
# not more: a tenth hue pushes the normal-vision floor below the readable
# threshold. The thin white segment borders supply the secondary encoding that a
# CVD dE in the 6-8 band requires. Thelebolus deliberately reuses the
# dung-saprotroph orange -- it IS panel B's dominant dung saprotroph -- and grey
# #999999 likewise carries "no assignment" in both panels.
genus_cols <- setNames(
  c("#E69F00", "#8C3800", "#F0E442", "#228833", "#66CCEE",
    "#4B0055", "#AA4499", "#003D30", "#FFAABB", "#EEEEEE", "#999999"), GEN_LEVELS)
guild_cols <- c("Dung saprotroph" = "#E69F00", "Plant-associated" = "#009E73",
                "Pathotroph" = "#CC79A7", "Other assigned" = "#56B4E9",
                "Unassigned / dark" = "#999999")
season_cols <- c(Winter = "#0072B2", Summer = "#D55E00")

italicise <- function(x) ifelse(grepl("unclass\\.|^Other |^Unassigned", x), x,
                                paste0("*", x, "*"))
base_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.tag         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.8, "lines"),
        legend.key.size  = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text      = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 9))
n_lab <- setNames(paste0(levels(Season), " (n = ", table(Season), ")"), levels(Season))

stacked <- function(dat, cols, title, labels = names(cols)) {
  ggplot(dat, aes(SampleID, share, fill = Category)) +
    geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.12,
             position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    facet_grid(~ Season, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x",
               labeller = labeller(Season = n_lab)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = cols, labels = labels, name = title) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    base_theme +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
}

# ---- panels A and B --------------------------------------------------------
pA <- stacked(genL, genus_cols, "Genus", italicise(GEN_LEVELS)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Read share") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1, order = 1))
# B repeats A's sample axis exactly, so its facet strips are dropped as redundant.
pB <- stacked(guiL, guild_cols, "Functional guild") +
  labs(x = "Dung sample (ordered within season by dung-saprotroph share)",
       y = "Read share") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1, order = 2)) +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank())

# ---- panel C: guild read share by season, BH-adjusted Wilcoxon -------------
season_stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(GUILD_LEVELS, function(g) {
  wt <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(guild_share[Season == "Summer", g],
                                     guild_share[Season == "Winter", g]))
  data.frame(Guild = g, p_value = wt$p.value, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
season_stats$q_value <- p.adjust(season_stats$p_value, method = "BH")
sig_lab <- function(q) ifelse(q < 0.001, "***", ifelse(q < 0.01, "**",
                       ifelse(q < 0.05, "*", "ns")))
ann <- data.frame(Category = factor(GUILD_LEVELS, levels = GUILD_LEVELS),
                  y = 1.04, lab = sig_lab(season_stats$q_value))
wrap_lab <- setNames(c("Dung\nsaprotroph", "Plant-\nassociated", "Pathotroph",
                       "Other\nassigned", "Unassigned\n/ dark"), GUILD_LEVELS)

pC <- ggplot(guiL, aes(Category, share, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.65, alpha = 0.85,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.12, dodge.width = 0.75,
                                             seed = 1),
             size = 0.9, alpha = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = ann, aes(Category, y, label = lab), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols, name = "Season") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = wrap_lab) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.09),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Per-sample read share") +
  base_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1, order = 3))

# ---- assemble and write ----------------------------------------------------
fig1 <- (pA / pB / pC) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1, 1.15), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.justification = "top")

# Every main figure is written three ways: PNG and JPG (600 dpi raster, for
# submission systems that demand one or the other) and PDF (vector, for print).
save_fig <- function(stem, obj, width, height, res = 600) {
  one <- function(open_dev) { open_dev(); on.exit(grDevices::dev.off()); print(obj) }
  one(function() grDevices::png(paste0(stem, ".png"), width = width, height = height,
                                units = "in", res = res))
  one(function() grDevices::jpeg(paste0(stem, ".jpg"), width = width, height = height,
                                 units = "in", res = res, quality = 95))
  pdf_dev <- if (capabilities("cairo")) grDevices::cairo_pdf else grDevices::pdf
  one(function() pdf_dev(paste0(stem, ".pdf"), width = width, height = height))
}
save_fig(file.path(out_dir, "Fig1_composition_function"), fig1, 10, 11)

cat(sprintf("Top %d genera (mean per-sample read share, %%):\n", N_GENERA))
print(round(100 * colMeans(gen_share), 2))
cat("\nGuild read share by season (mean %) and BH q:\n")
print(data.frame(Guild  = GUILD_LEVELS,
                 summer = round(100 * colMeans(guild_share[Season == "Summer", ]), 1),
                 winter = round(100 * colMeans(guild_share[Season == "Winter", ]), 1),
                 q      = signif(season_stats$q_value, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

### 10.2 Figure 2 — Seasonal turnover and its year-to-year variation (H1)

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
*Provenance: Fig. 2A is the ordination of Section 4.1; Fig. 2B the distance-to-Season-centroid model of Section 4.3. Test statistics are read from the committed `tables/report_permanova.csv` and `tables/report_centroid_lm.csv`, so the figure cannot drift from Section 4.*
::::

![](figures/main/Fig2_seasonal_turnover.png)

**Figure 2**: Winter and summer dung mycobiomes differ in composition, and the size of that difference varies among years. **(A)** Unconstrained principal coordinates analysis of robust Aitchison distances among the 52 canonical samples, coloured by season and shaped by year. Thin lines join each sample to its season centroid (×). The axis percentages are shares of the rank-3 reconstruction from which `vegan` computes robust Aitchison distances, not of the full community variation, and the axis titles name that denominator accordingly; under a full-rank Aitchison distance (CLR after a pseudocount) the same two axes take **13.7% and 9.5%**, which is the closer approximation to the variance actually explained (Appendix Section 4.1). **(B)** Distance of each sample to its own season centroid in robust-CLR space, split by season and year; boxes show the median and interquartile range and points are individual samples. Subtitles give the PERMANOVA terms (A) and the ANOVA terms of the `distance ~ Season × Year` model of within-season spread (B).

Winter and summer communities separate along the first ordination axis: Season explains 11% of compositional variance (PERMANOVA p = 0.002; Table S5). The seasonal contrast is not, however, demonstrably of constant size — the Season × Year interaction is significant (R² = 0.10, p = 0.011), as it is under three of the four alternative distances, though only marginal under the zeros-retained robust CLR (p = 0.061; Table S7b). The per-year tests make the shift much the largest in 2023 (R² = 0.14–0.24, p ≤ 0.009 under every distance), with smaller contrasts in 2024 (R² = 0.09–0.14) and 2022 (R² = 0.07–0.10), each significant under three of the five distances (Tables S5b, S7c). What survives every distance measure is the *ordering* of the three years rather than the size of the gap between them: under the rank-3 robust Aitchison distance of panel A the 2022 contrast alone collapses to R² = 0.02 (p = 0.789), an artefact of the truncated distance rather than a year without a seasonal shift (Section 4.2, caveat iii). Panel B shows that this is a difference in *where* the seasons sit rather than in how tightly each clusters: summer samples are consistently further from their own centroid than winter samples in every year (Season p \< 0.001), with no Season × Year interaction in that spread (p = 0.79). Two caveats belong with this figure and are treated in Section 4.2: summer samples are significantly more dispersed than winter ones, so part of the PERMANOVA R² reflects spread rather than location alone (Anderson 2001), and the axis percentages are shares of a rank-3 completion of the robust CLR matrix — panel A plots two of only three available dimensions, which is why its axis titles name that space rather than reporting a bare percentage (Section 4.1).

```{r fig2-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full build code for Figure 2 — the source of truth for figures/main/Fig2_seasonal_turnover.{png,jpg,pdf}"

# Figure 2 -- Seasonal turnover and its year-to-year variation (H1).
# Both panels reuse the Section 4 analysis verbatim (its build chunk in §4):
# panel A the unconstrained robust-Aitchison PCoA, panel B the distance-to-
# Season-centroid in rCLR space. Test statistics are READ from the committed
# tables/ CSVs so the figure and Section 4 can never drift apart.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig2-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(phyloseq); library(vegan); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})

rdata <- if (file.exists("eco_analysis.RData")) "eco_analysis.RData" else
         "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/trimmed/mergedPlates/eco_analysis.RData"
load(rdata)
tab_dir <- if (dir.exists("tables")) "tables" else
           "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/Scripts_server/Supplementary/tables"
out_dir <- "figures/main"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                  # headless: no X11 fallback

season_cols <- c(Winter = "#0072B2", Summer = "#D55E00")   # repo standard
# Fillable shapes (21/24/22, not 16/17/15) so BOTH panels map Season to `fill`
# and the two panels can share one Season key.
year_shapes <- c(`2022` = 21, `2023` = 24, `2024` = 22)
base_theme  <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.tag        = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        legend.key.size = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title    = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text     = element_text(size = 9))

# ---- data ------------------------------------------------------------------
ps      <- alldat$nopool                              # canonical, 52 samples
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(ps), "matrix"); if (taxa_are_rows(ps)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)
meta    <- data.frame(sample_data(ps), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(otu_mat), rownames(meta)))
Season  <- factor(c(winter = "Winter", summer = "Summer")[meta$Season],
                  levels = c("Winter", "Summer"))
Year    <- factor(meta$Year)
stopifnot(!anyNA(Season), !anyNA(Year))

# ---- panel A: unconstrained PCoA on robust Aitchison distances -------------
d_ait <- vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison")
attr(d_ait, "Labels") <- rownames(otu_mat)   # vegdist drops Labels for robust.aitchison
ord   <- capscale(d_ait ~ 1)
# Defensive only: this distance yields exactly 3 positive eigenvalues and no
# negative ones, because vegan's rclr completes the matrix at rank 3 (Section 4.1).
eig   <- pmax(ord$CA$eig, 0)
ax1p  <- round(100 * eig[1] / sum(eig), 1); ax2p <- round(100 * eig[2] / sum(eig), 1)

sc <- as.data.frame(scores(ord, display = "sites", choices = 1:2, scaling = 1))
colnames(sc)[1:2] <- c("Axis1", "Axis2")
sc$Season <- Season[match(rownames(sc), rownames(meta))]
sc$Year   <- Year[match(rownames(sc), rownames(meta))]
cent <- aggregate(cbind(Axis1, Axis2) ~ Season, data = sc, FUN = mean)
names(cent) <- c("Season", "cX", "cY")
sc <- merge(sc, cent, by = "Season")

perm <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
pr   <- perm[perm$term == "Season", ]
pi   <- perm[perm$term == "Season:Year", ]
by_y <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_permanova_by_year.csv"), check.names = FALSE)

pA <- ggplot(sc, aes(Axis1, Axis2)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = cX, yend = cY, colour = Season),
               alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Season, shape = Year), size = 2.8,
             colour = "grey25", stroke = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = cent, aes(cX, cY, colour = Season), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 4.5, shape = 4, stroke = 1.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = year_shapes) +
  coord_equal() +
  # See Section 4.1: these are shares of the rank-3 rCLR reconstruction, so the
  # denominator is named in the axis title rather than left to the caption.
  labs(x = sprintf("PCoA1 (%.1f%% of rank-3 rCLR space)", ax1p),
       y = sprintf("PCoA2 (%.1f%% of rank-3 rCLR space)", ax2p),
       subtitle = sprintf("PERMANOVA  Season: R² = %.2f, p = %.3f\nSeason × Year: R² = %.2f, p = %.3f",
                          pr$R2, pr$`Pr(>F)`, pi$R2, pi$`Pr(>F)`)) +
  base_theme +
  guides(fill  = guide_legend(order = 1, override.aes = list(shape = 21, size = 3)),
         shape = guide_legend(order = 2, override.aes = list(fill = "grey45", size = 3)))

# ---- panel B: distance to Season centroid, by Season x Year ----------------
rclr <- decostand(otu_mat, "rclr", MARGIN = 1)
dimnames(rclr) <- dimnames(otu_mat)          # vegan's rclr path drops dimnames
centroids <- rowsum(rclr, group = meta$Season) / as.vector(table(meta$Season))
euclid <- function(x, y) sqrt(sum((x - y)^2))
dcent <- data.frame(
  Season = Season, Year = Year,
  dist   = vapply(seq_len(nrow(rclr)),
                  function(k) euclid(rclr[k, ], centroids[meta$Season[k], ]), numeric(1)))

lmres <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "report_centroid_lm.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
pfmt  <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else sprintf("p = %.2f", p)
p_sea <- lmres$`Pr(>F)`[lmres$term == "Season"]
p_int <- lmres$`Pr(>F)`[lmres$term == "Season:Year"]

pB <- ggplot(dcent, aes(Year, dist, fill = Season)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.65, alpha = 0.85,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.75,
                                             seed = 1),
             size = 1.3, alpha = 0.7, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distance to season centroid (rCLR)",
       subtitle = sprintf("Within-season spread\nSeason: %s;  Season × Year: %s",
                          pfmt(p_sea), pfmt(p_int))) +
  base_theme +
  # Panel A already carries the Season key; a second one would not merge with it
  # (different key glyph) and would just be printed twice.
  guides(fill = "none")

# ---- assemble and write ----------------------------------------------------
fig2 <- (pA | pB) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal")

# Every main figure is written three ways: PNG and JPG (600 dpi raster, for
# submission systems that demand one or the other) and PDF (vector, for print).
save_fig <- function(stem, obj, width, height, res = 600) {
  one <- function(open_dev) { open_dev(); on.exit(grDevices::dev.off()); print(obj) }
  one(function() grDevices::png(paste0(stem, ".png"), width = width, height = height,
                                units = "in", res = res))
  one(function() grDevices::jpeg(paste0(stem, ".jpg"), width = width, height = height,
                                 units = "in", res = res, quality = 95))
  pdf_dev <- if (capabilities("cairo")) grDevices::cairo_pdf else grDevices::pdf
  one(function() pdf_dev(paste0(stem, ".pdf"), width = width, height = height))
}
save_fig(file.path(out_dir, "Fig2_seasonal_turnover"), fig2, 10, 5.4)

cat(sprintf("PCoA axes: %.1f%% / %.1f%%\n", ax1p, ax2p))
cat(sprintf("PERMANOVA Season R2 = %.3f, p = %.3f\n", pr$R2, pr$`Pr(>F)`))
cat("Mean distance to season centroid:\n")
print(round(tapply(dcent$dist, list(dcent$Season, dcent$Year), mean), 1))
```

### 10.3 Figure 3 — A reproducible seasonal axis inside large among-individual variation (HMSC synthesis)

:::: {.content-visible when-profile="docs"}
*Provenance: both panels of Fig. 3 come from the same abundance (CLR) HMSC model of Section 9. Fig. 3A is the per-OTU seasonal niche of Section 9.4 (Tables S-HMSCe(i) and S-HMSCe(ii)), restricted to the 22 OTUs that each hold at least 1% of modelled read share and augmented with a guild-mean block; Figure S-HMSCc is the same quantity for all 226 OTUs ranked by effect size rather than by abundance. Fig. 3B is the variance partition of Section 9.2 (Table S-HMSCc); its right-hand column is the model-free PCR-replicate share of Table S-HMSCc2 (`tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance.csv`). The read shares behind the selection rule come from `tables/dark_taxa_SH_matching.csv` (Section 3.4), which is also the source of the finest-rank labels for OTUs with no genus. Both panels read committed `tables/*.csv` written by `10_hmsc.R` and `9_dark_taxa_SH_matching.R`, so the figure cannot drift from Sections 9 and 3.4.*
::::

![](figures/main/Fig3_hmsc_synthesis.png)

<!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29 (caption rewritten for the revised model): rewrite freely -->
**Figure 3**: A joint species distribution model places the seasonal axis at OTU level and sizes it against the variation among individual droppings. Both panels come from one abundance (CLR) HMSC model fitted to 226 OTUs in 55 droppings, with each dropping's two PCR replicates averaged, Season and Year as fixed effects, and the dropping as random level (Section 9.1). **(A)** Per-OTU Season coefficient in CLR units — positive = higher relative abundance in summer — for the 22 OTUs that each account for at least 1% of modelled-OTU read share, 73% of all modelled reads between them, ordered by coefficient and coloured by functional guild, with 95% credible intervals. One interval, OTU1369's, extends beyond the axis and is clipped at −6 with an arrowhead (it reaches −6.48). Filled points are the 16 resolved at HMSC's 0.95 posterior-support convention; community-wide, 74 of 226 OTUs have a 95% credible interval excluding zero. The lower block gives each guild's arithmetic mean of the per-OTU posterior means (diamond) with their interquartile range, taken over all OTUs in that guild rather than only the 22 plotted; it is a descriptive summary of the points above, not a credible interval. The model's own guild-level estimate is the trait-level Gamma (Section 9.3, Table S-HMSCd2). The four MCMC chains agree on every plotted estimate (Beta PSRF ≤ 1.01; Table S-HMSCb). **(B)** Mean share of per-OTU explained variance attributed to Season, Year and the dropping, for all 226 OTUs and then within each guild (Table S-HMSCc). The italic right-hand column is not part of that partition. It is the share of each OTU's total CLR variance that lies between the two PCR replicates of a dropping, measured outside the model (Table S-HMSCc2), and it mostly reflects rare taxa detected by one replicate but not the other. The three highlighted rows are drawn larger because they are the groups this study is about. The five guild classes are the model's trait and differ slightly from the display split used in Figure 1: 46 OTUs carrying a genus but no FUNGuild call sit in "Other assigned" here and in "Unassigned / dark" there (`tables/guild_scheme_crosswalk.csv`, Section 8.1).

Panel A makes the seasonal signal concrete at the level of individual lineages, and it does so among the taxa that actually constitute the community: the 22 OTUs plotted are every OTU holding at least 1% of modelled read share, and they carry 73% of the modelled reads between them. <!-- CLAUDE DRAFT 2026-09-29 (numbers and claims updated to the revised model): rewrite freely -->
Read from the top, the panel is the study's taxonomic result in one column. The summer end is an unbroken block of coprophilous dung saprotrophs — *Thelebolus* (OTU1, β = +4.17), *Sporormiella* (OTU636, +3.52), *Coniochaeta* (OTU1225, +3.44) and two further Sporormiaceae and Coniochaetaceae lineages — every one of them resolved. The winter end is a block dominated by dark, taxonomically unresolved taxa, ending at OTU1369 (−5.00), the unclassified Dothideomycete that dominates winter read share in Figure 5. Plant-associated taxa straddle zero between them. The guild means below make the same statement over all 226 OTUs rather than the 22 shown. Dung saprotrophs (+1.32) have by far the most summer-shifted mean; dark/unassigned taxa (−0.31) and pathotrophs (−0.33) lean winter; and the yeast-rich "other" group is weakly positive (+0.22). The model's trait-level estimate agrees: the dung-saprotroph guild's Season effect is positive with posterior support 0.994, and dark/unassigned, pathotroph and plant-associated OTUs respond clearly less summer-ward (Section 9.3). Panel B sizes these effects. Season accounts for 31.5% of the variance the model explains and Year for 18.5%, while half (49.9%) sits among droppings — one dropping to the next. The Season share is largest for dung saprotrophs (49.8%): coprophiles are the taxa whose abundance season determines most. Measured separately, a further 32% of total CLR variance is replicate-to-replicate noise within a dropping, most of it whether rare taxa are detected at all; coprophiles are the most repeatable guild (17%). Taken together the panels state the central quantitative claim in one place: seasonal turnover is real, directional and consistent across methods, yet it sits beside large idiosyncrasy among individual droppings — which is why the model explains the samples it has seen (R² ≈ 0.29) but predicts held-out droppings far less well (cross-validated R² ≈ 0.03; Section 9.7).

```{r fig3-build}
#| eval: false
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Full build code for Figure 3 — the source of truth for figures/main/Fig3_hmsc_synthesis.{png,jpg,pdf}"

# Figure 3 -- HMSC synthesis: per-OTU seasonal niche + variance partition.
# Every number is READ from committed tables/ CSVs; no model is loaded or
# refitted here (the fits are ~200 MB each and the figure needs only their
# posterior summaries).
#   A  tables/hmsc_beta_season.csv         (per-OTU Season Beta, CLR abundance)
#      tables/dark_taxa_SH_matching.csv    (per-OTU read share + full lineage)
#   B  tables/hmsc_variance_partition.csv  (per-OTU variance components, CLR)
#      tables/hmsc_pcr_replicate_variance.csv (model-free PCR-replicate share)
#      tables/hmsc_convergence_psrf.csv    (quoted in the caption, checked here)
#
# BOTH panels are the headline ABUNDANCE (CLR) model: CLR averaged over each
# dropping's two PCR replicates, one row per dropping, biological sample as the
# random level (Section 9.1; revised 2026-09-29 -- the previous uncapped
# replicate-level model did not converge). The occurrence (probit) model is a
# supplementary robustness check (Section 9.4, Tables S-HMSCe(iii)/(iv)) and is
# deliberately NOT mixed into this figure: on the occurrence scale the whole
# community shifts summer-ward (157/226 OTUs positive), which ranks rare taxa at
# the extremes and puts "other assigned" ahead of dung saprotrophs -- a richness
# result already carried by Figure 4.
# Rebuild:  conda run -n r_env Rscript build_main_figure.R fig3-build

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2); library(patchwork); library(ggtext)
})

tab_dir <- if (dir.exists("tables")) "tables" else
           "/home/daniel/Ptarmigan/Scripts_server/Supplementary/tables"
out_dir <- "figures/main"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
grDevices::pdf(NULL)                                 # headless: no X11 fallback

# ---- shared style ----------------------------------------------------------
# Guild colours are Figure 1's, so a guild is the same colour in every main
# figure. The model's five-level trait is NOT identical to Figure 1's display
# split (46 OTUs move between "Other assigned" and "Unassigned / dark"); the
# caption says so and tables/guild_scheme_crosswalk.csv reconciles them.
GUILD_LEVELS <- c("Dung saprotroph", "Plant-associated", "Pathotroph",
                  "Other assigned", "Unassigned / dark")
guild_cols <- c("Dung saprotroph" = "#E69F00", "Plant-associated" = "#009E73",
                "Pathotroph" = "#CC79A7", "Other assigned" = "#56B4E9",
                "Unassigned / dark" = "#999999")
guild_map <- c(dung_saprotroph = "Dung saprotroph", plant_associated = "Plant-associated",
               pathotroph = "Pathotroph", other = "Other assigned",
               dark_unassigned = "Unassigned / dark")
# Variance components deliberately share NO colour with the guild scale, and
# split fixed (coloured) from random (grey): the visual point of panel B is how
# little of the bar is coloured.
# The headline model averages PCR replicates, so it has NO PCR random level;
# PCR-replicate variance is drawn as a separate, model-free column (panel B).
VP_LEVELS <- c("Season", "Year", "Random: sample")   # CSV column names
# Displayed names: the CSV's terse "Random: sample" is fine in a supplementary
# table but a main-text key has to say what the level actually is.
vp_display <- c("Season" = "Season", "Year" = "Year",
                "Random: sample" = "Biological sample (dropping)")
vp_cols <- c("Season" = "#0072B2", "Year" = "#F0E442",
             "Biological sample (dropping)" = "#666666")

base_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y     = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.5, angle = 0),
        plot.tag         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
        panel.spacing    = unit(0.5, "lines"),
        legend.key.size  = unit(0.42, "cm"),
        legend.title     = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.text      = element_text(size = 9))

# All in-plot text is ASCII: save_fig() falls back to grDevices::pdf when cairo
# is unavailable, and that device silently substitutes a dot for a Unicode glyph.
# (The markdown asterisks below are ggtext italics markup, and are ASCII.)

strip_rank <- function(x) sub("^[a-z]__", "", x)

# ============================================================================
# Panel A -- per-OTU seasonal niche (CLR abundance), plus guild means
# ============================================================================
b <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "hmsc_beta_season.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(b) == 226L, !anyNA(b$beta_season_mean), !anyNA(b$beta_season_CrI2.5),
          !anyNA(b$beta_season_support), setequal(b$guild, names(guild_map)))
b$Guild <- factor(unname(guild_map[b$guild]), levels = GUILD_LEVELS)

# Read share AND full lineage both come from the E1 per-OTU table (Section 3.4),
# the one committed file carrying a complete Kingdom..Species lineage together
# with per-season mean read shares for every OTU in the study. Using it here is
# what lets an OTU with no genus be labelled by its finest resolved rank
# ("Dothideomycetes (OTU1369)") instead of a bare, unreadable ID.
sh <- read.csv(file.path(tab_dir, "dark_taxa_SH_matching.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(sh) == 1129L, all(b$OTU_ID %in% sh$OTU_ID), !any(duplicated(sh$OTU_ID)))
si <- match(b$OTU_ID, sh$OTU_ID)
# Guard: the Beta table's own Genus column must agree with the lineage source,
# or the labels would be describing different OTUs than the estimates.
stopifnot(all(is.na(b$Genus) == is.na(sh$Genus[si])),
          all(strip_rank(sh$Genus[si]) == b$Genus, na.rm = TRUE))

# winter_mean_share and summer_mean_share are each a mean over that season's
# samples, so their unweighted average is the OTU's mean share of a dropping.
# Renormalising over the 226 MODELLED OTUs (not all 1129) is what makes "1% of
# read share" a statement about the community the model actually sees.
b$share <- (sh$winter_mean_share[si] + sh$summer_mean_share[si]) / 2
stopifnot(!anyNA(b$share), all(b$share >= 0), sum(b$share) > 0)
b$rel <- b$share / sum(b$share)

# Selection rule: a stated threshold rather than an arbitrary top-N, so the
# panel's membership is reproducible and cannot be read as cherry-picked. It
# also ties Figure 3 to Figure 1, which is likewise read-share weighted.
SHARE_MIN <- 0.01
sel <- b[b$rel >= SHARE_MIN, ]
sel <- sel[order(-sel$beta_season_mean), ]
sel_cov <- sum(sel$rel)
stopifnot(nrow(sel) == 22L, sel_cov > 0.70, sel_cov < 0.76)

# Row labels: finest resolved rank, genus italicised via ggtext. Incertae sedis
# placeholders are not genera and are shown at the rank they actually resolve to.
RANKS <- c("Genus", "Family", "Order", "Class", "Phylum")
label_one <- function(i, otu) {
  v  <- strip_rank(unlist(sh[i, RANKS], use.names = FALSE))
  ok <- which(!is.na(v) & nzchar(v))
  if (!length(ok)) return(paste0("Fungi (", otu, ")"))
  k <- ok[1]
  nm <- sub("_(gen|fam|ord|cls)_Incertae_sedis$", "", v[k])
  if (k == 1L && !grepl("Incertae", v[k], fixed = TRUE)) nm <- paste0("*", nm, "*")
  paste0(nm, " (", otu, ")")
}
sel$lab <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(sel)),
                  function(j) label_one(match(sel$OTU_ID[j], sh$OTU_ID), sel$OTU_ID[j]),
                  character(1))
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(sel$lab)))

# Resolution marker: HMSC's own convention -- one-sided posterior support of
# 0.95, i.e. a 90% two-sided interval. The caption also reports how many OTUs
# community-wide have a 95% CrI excluding zero, so the weaker criterion is not
# passed off as the stronger.
SUPP <- 0.95
sel$resolved <- factor(
  ifelse(sel$beta_season_support >= SUPP | sel$beta_season_support <= 1 - SUPP,
         "Posterior support >= 0.95", "Not resolved"),
  levels = c("Posterior support >= 0.95", "Not resolved"))
n_res <- sum(sel$resolved == "Posterior support >= 0.95")

# Guild means over ALL OTUs of that guild (not just the 22 plotted), with the
# IQR of the same per-OTU estimates as a spread -- a summary of the points
# above, NOT a credible interval, which is why it is drawn as a plain segment.
gm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(GUILD_LEVELS, function(g) {
  v <- b$beta_season_mean[b$Guild == g]
  data.frame(Guild = factor(g, levels = GUILD_LEVELS), n = length(v),
             mean = mean(v), q25 = quantile(v, 0.25), q75 = quantile(v, 0.75),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
gm$lab <- sprintf("%s (n = %d)", as.character(gm$Guild), gm$n)

# Drift guard against the committed per-OTU table itself -- guild sizes and
# guild means -- which is what the panel actually draws. (These are means of
# per-OTU posterior means in CLR units, NOT the trait-level Gamma, which is on
# the standardised scale and reported in Section 9.3.)
N_EXP  <- c("Dung saprotroph" = 14L, "Plant-associated" = 50L, "Pathotroph" = 16L,
            "Other assigned" = 67L, "Unassigned / dark" = 79L)
GM_EXP <- c("Dung saprotroph" = 1.320, "Plant-associated" = -0.095, "Pathotroph" = -0.332,
            "Other assigned" = 0.223, "Unassigned / dark" = -0.312)
gm_n <- setNames(gm$n, as.character(gm$Guild))
gm_m <- setNames(gm$mean, as.character(gm$Guild))
stopifnot(sum(N_EXP) == 226L, all(gm_n[names(N_EXP)] == N_EXP),
          max(abs(gm_m[names(GM_EXP)] - GM_EXP)) < 0.01,
          as.character(gm$Guild[which.max(gm$mean)]) == "Dung saprotroph")

# One plot, two blocks: facet_grid with free space gives the guild block a
```
